guides.caption: The zero value comes from the type, not from leftover memory.

nodes.detail: Starts at ""; bool starts at false
nodes.label: Text and flags

nodes.detail: Pointers, slices, maps and channels start nil
nodes.label: References

guides.practical: Design a type so its zero value is useful when possible. A zero counter can be incremented and a nil slice can be appended to. A nil map can be read, but needs allocation before a write; a nil channel blocks both sends and receives.
guides.title: A value exists before you assign one
guides.watchOut: Zero does not mean ready for every operation. Check the rules of the specific type before using it.

guides.caption: Short declarations are for local variables; package-level declarations use var.

nodes.detail: Creates a name in this block
nodes.label: Declare

nodes.detail: At least one name must be new
nodes.label: Mixed declaration

guides.practical: Read a short declaration together with its block. Inside a nested if or for block, the same spelling may introduce a different variable. A short declaration with multiple names may reuse names from that same block when at least one other name is new.
guides.title: Creation and reassignment are different steps
guides.watchOut: An inner `err :=` can shadow an outer `err`. Use `=` when you intend to update an existing variable.

guides.caption: The signature makes the failure path visible at the call site.
guides.practical: Keep the failure branch short, then let the successful path continue without extra nesting. Give the error context at the boundary where you know what operation was attempted. A function may return a useful partial result with an error only when its contract explicitly says so.
guides.title: Check the error before using the value
guides.watchOut: Discarding an error with `_` does not handle it. Make that choice only when the operation is known to be safe.

guides.caption: Go checks unused imports per file and unused local variables at compile time.

nodes.detail: A file must use its imports
nodes.label: Import

nodes.detail: A declared local must be used
nodes.label: Local variable

nodes.detail: The blank identifier names no variable
nodes.label: Intentional discard

guides.practical: During a repair, decide whether the unused value belongs in the result or should be removed. Keep imports close to the code that needs them. The blank identifier is useful for an intentionally ignored result, but removing dead work usually makes the program clearer.
guides.title: Every local name needs a purpose
guides.watchOut: A blank assignment only satisfies the compiler. It does not explain why calculating an unused value was necessary.

guides.caption: Constant arithmetic is exact until a typed operation imposes a representation.
guides.practical: Use typed constants when a public API needs a particular type; keep untyped constants flexible when callers may use different numeric types. In a const block, iota counts specifications, including a blank-identifier specification. Several names on one specification share the same iota value.
guides.title: A constant gets a type when the context asks
guides.watchOut: A constant can be valid by itself and still overflow the type of the variable or argument receiving it.

guides.caption: An expressionless switch is a sequence of conditions, not a loop.
guides.practical: Put more specific conditions before broader ones. Several values can share one case, so avoid repeating an identical body. A break can explicitly leave a switch early, but no break is needed merely to stop at the end of a case.
guides.title: The first matching case finishes the switch
guides.watchOut: `fallthrough` runs the next case body without testing its condition. Use it only when that behavior is intentional.

guides.caption: Equal storage widths do not make two numeric types interchangeable.

nodes.detail: A named type protects a meaning
nodes.label: Distinct types

guides.practical: Choose the result type before choosing a conversion. Converting an integer to a float can lose precision for large values; converting a float to an integer truncates the fractional part. An explicit conversion documents the decision, but it does not make a lossy conversion harmless.
guides.title: Make the type change visible
guides.watchOut: Check an empty collection before dividing by its length. Type correctness alone does not prevent division by zero.

guides.caption: A bare return returns the current named result values.

nodes.detail: Explicit values keep the exit clear
nodes.label: Return

guides.practical: Use result names when they explain a pair of similar types, such as a lower and upper bound. They begin at their zero values and remain in scope for the body. An explicit return is often easier to review than a bare return once the function has branches.
guides.title: Named results are local variables
guides.watchOut: A deferred closure can change named results before the caller receives them. That is useful, but deserves a visible contract.

guides.caption: Registration order and execution order point in opposite directions.

nodes.detail: This call is stacked above A
nodes.label: Register second

nodes.detail: The newest deferred call runs first
nodes.label: Return

guides.practical: Put cleanup next to successful acquisition so later return paths cannot bypass it. The function and arguments of a deferred call are evaluated when defer executes; a deferred closure can instead read variables later. This difference explains many surprising loop and mutation examples.
guides.title: Deferred work unwinds in reverse order
guides.watchOut: Defer runs when the surrounding function returns, not at the end of an inner block or one loop iteration.

guides.caption: A struct value carries its fields together; assigning it copies that value.

nodes.code: type Point struct { X, Y int }
nodes.label: Type

guides.practical: Prefer keyed literals when the field meanings are not obvious. An omitted field is deliberately zero, which is helpful for configuration structs. A struct copy is shallow: slice, map and pointer fields still refer to the same backing data even though the outer struct is a new value.
guides.title: Field names make construction readable
guides.watchOut: A copied struct containing a mutex must not be used as an independent lock after the original lock has been used.

guides.caption: The receiver is an explicit part of the method declaration.

nodes.detail: The receiver type owns the method
nodes.label: Value

nodes.detail: A pointer receiver can mutate c
nodes.label: Method

nodes.detail: The receiver supplies the first operand
nodes.label: Call

guides.practical: Choose pointer receivers when a method needs to change the receiver or when copying the value would be inappropriate. Keep receiver naming short and consistent across methods. Whether a value satisfies an interface is decided by its method set, which is a separate rule from convenient call syntax.
guides.title: A receiver gives a function a home
guides.watchOut: Go may take the address of an addressable value for a method call. That convenience does not add pointer methods to its value method set.

guides.caption: Assigning through either pointer changes the one shared value.
guides.practical: Use a pointer to communicate shared identity or a permitted mutation. A pointer is itself copied when passed to a function, so reassigning the parameter changes only that local pointer; assigning through it changes the pointed-to value. Check nil before dereferencing an optional pointer.
guides.title: Two names can reach one value
guides.watchOut: A pointer does not automatically make code faster. Allocation and copying behavior depend on the program and compiler.

guides.caption: Calls to one returned closure share its captured variables.
guides.practical: A closure is a useful way to return a small stateful operation without exposing a struct. Separate calls to the factory create separate captured state. Multiple closures created in one environment may share that state, so concurrent use still needs synchronization.
guides.title: The function keeps access to its environment
guides.watchOut: Capturing a variable does not freeze its current value. Copy it deliberately when the callback needs a snapshot.

guides.caption: Go keeps reachable values alive; a returned pointer is not a dangling reference.

nodes.detail: The function creates a local value
nodes.label: Create

guides.practical: Escape analysis decides where storage can live while preserving language semantics. Returning a pointer to a local is safe, but it may require heap storage. Prefer the API shape that expresses ownership and optionality clearly, then inspect allocation behavior if a measured hot path needs improvement.
guides.title: The value outlives the returning function
guides.watchOut: Safe lifetime does not mean synchronized access. Sharing the returned pointer across goroutines still requires coordination.

guides.caption: Length is the current view; capacity is the room available behind that view.

nodes.detail: The reslicing limit from this start
nodes.label: Reserved storage

nodes.detail: May reuse or replace the backing array
nodes.label: Growth

guides.practical: Use make with a capacity estimate when building a result incrementally. An append returns the updated slice header, so retain that returned value. The growth policy is an implementation detail; correct code must not depend on a particular capacity after an allocation.
guides.title: A slice sees part of a backing array
guides.watchOut: Capacity does not permit indexing beyond length. Reslice first when exposing an existing part of the backing array.

guides.caption: Copying a slice copies its header, not its elements.

nodes.detail: Has its own length and capacity
nodes.label: View A

nodes.detail: Overlapping elements refer to the same storage
nodes.label: View B

guides.practical: Decide whether a function returns a view or an independent copy. Use copy or slices.Clone when callers must not share mutations. A full slice expression can restrict capacity and force a later append to allocate, but it does not detach elements already visible in the slice.
guides.title: Slice headers can share one backing array
guides.watchOut: An append that fits capacity may overwrite values visible through another slice. An append that reallocates has different sharing behavior.

guides.caption: A safe read does not imply that a map is allocated for writes.

nodes.detail: Reads return the value type zero
nodes.label: Nil map

guides.practical: Initialize a map at the point where a function takes responsibility for storing entries. Use the two-result lookup when an absent key must be distinguished from a stored zero. Deleting a key from a nil map is safe, but assignment to a nil map panics.
guides.title: Reading and writing have different requirements
guides.watchOut: Maps are not safe for unsynchronized concurrent reads and writes. Protect access or transfer ownership.

guides.caption: A rune is a code point; a user-visible character may contain several runes.
guides.practical: Choose the unit the operation actually needs. Protocols often need byte offsets; Unicode processing often needs runes. Range over a string yields the byte offset and the decoded rune, so its indexes are not a consecutive rune counter.
guides.title: Bytes and Unicode code points are different views
guides.watchOut: Counting runes is still not counting displayed characters. Combining marks and emoji sequences can contain multiple code points.

guides.caption: The range loop and yield call cooperate to stop at the same boundary.
guides.practical: Keep iterator state local unless reuse is intentionally stateful. A rangeable function may yield no values, one value, or a key and value, according to its signature. As soon as yield returns false, stop calling it and release any resources owned by the iterator.
guides.title: The iterator offers values through yield
guides.watchOut: Calling yield again after it returned false violates the iterator protocol and can panic.

guides.caption: Both operations are checked; capacity is not an indexing permission.
guides.practical: Check bounds at the boundary where external indexes enter your program. A sub-slice capacity starts at its own first element, not at the original array beginning. A full slice expression is useful when passing a view to code that may append without permission to overwrite later elements.
guides.title: Indexing and reslicing use different limits
guides.watchOut: Restricting capacity prevents append from using later storage; it does not prevent writes to elements already in the view.

guides.caption: The language does not specify map iteration order.
guides.practical: Use sorted keys for reports, snapshots, stable tests and serialized text. Test membership independently of order when order is irrelevant. An iteration may use a different order on the next pass; seeing one repeated order in a small example does not establish a guarantee.
guides.title: Sort keys when output order matters
guides.watchOut: Do not describe map traversal as insertion order or rely on a particular random distribution.

guides.caption: A builder avoids repeatedly concatenating an ever-growing prefix.
guides.practical: Use strings.Join when all pieces are already collected; use strings.Builder when generating text step by step. Grow can reserve a known size, but it is optional. A builder is for text, while bytes.Buffer is useful when both byte-oriented reads and writes are needed.
guides.title: Accumulate bytes before producing the string
guides.watchOut: Do not copy a non-zero strings.Builder. Keep one owner and measure before adding speculative capacity estimates.

guides.caption: make returns a slice, map or channel; new returns a pointer.

nodes.detail: A usable slice with three zero elements
nodes.label: Slice

nodes.detail: Returns a pointer to a zero int
nodes.label: Pointer

guides.practical: Pick the form that matches the value your API needs. A struct literal often expresses initialization more clearly than new. A pointer to a nil map is still a pointer to a nil map: allocating the pointer does not initialize the map it points to.
guides.title: Allocation and initialization answer different questions
guides.watchOut: `new([]int)` yields a pointer to a nil slice. It does not allocate any slice elements.

guides.caption: Arrays are values; slices describe a view over elements.

nodes.detail: A slice refers to backing storage
nodes.label: Flexible view

guides.practical: Use arrays when a fixed length is part of the contract, such as a digest. Array assignment copies every element. Slicing an array creates a view of it; converting or copying into another array is a separate operation with its own bounds requirements.
guides.title: Array length belongs to its type
guides.watchOut: Passing an array by value copies it. A slice parameter does not copy its backing elements.

guides.caption: The boolean answers whether the key exists, independently of the value.
guides.practical: Use comma-ok when zero is a meaningful stored value. The same pattern appears in type assertions and channel receives, but the boolean answers a different presence question in each case. Give it a name such as found when that improves the branch.
guides.title: Presence is a second result
guides.watchOut: Testing `v == 0` cannot distinguish an absent key from an entry explicitly containing zero.

guides.caption: Nil and empty slices behave alike for length, range and append.

nodes.detail: An empty slice runs zero iterations
nodes.label: Use

guides.practical: Return a nil slice when no results is a natural zero value, unless the API requires a non-nil empty value. Most callers should inspect length rather than compare to nil. Encoders may distinguish the two representations, so document the serialized contract when it matters.
guides.title: A nil slice already supports empty operations
guides.watchOut: The standard encoding/json package encodes a nil slice as null and a non-nil empty slice as [].

guides.caption: Named functions and closures can satisfy the same function type.

nodes.detail: Names the input and output types
nodes.label: Function value

guides.practical: Pass a function when callers should choose one operation without defining a whole object. A closure can adapt an existing function or capture small configuration. Keep the signature narrow so it is easy to test; a function value may be nil, so establish whether nil is allowed.
guides.title: A signature is a contract you can pass
guides.watchOut: A nil function value can be compared to nil, but calling it panics. Other function values cannot be compared for equality.

guides.caption: No implements declaration connects the type to the interface.
guides.practical: Define the interface next to the function that consumes it, using only the methods that function needs. Existing types can then satisfy it without knowing about your package. A compile-time assignment to the interface is a useful way to document and check a type intended to satisfy it.
guides.title: The consumer defines the behavior it needs
guides.watchOut: Method names alone are insufficient. Parameter and result types must match the interface signature exactly.

guides.caption: Convenient method-call syntax does not change interface satisfaction.

nodes.detail: The assigned type must supply Write
nodes.label: Interface check

guides.practical: When an interface assignment fails, inspect the type of the assigned expression and the receiver of each required method. An addressable local value may call a pointer method through automatic addressing; that same value still lacks the pointer method in its own method set.
guides.title: Value and pointer types have different method sets
guides.watchOut: Map elements are not addressable. Store pointers in the map or copy, modify and assign a value back.

guides.caption: Both parts must be absent for the interface itself to be nil.

nodes.detail: No dynamic type and no value
nodes.label: Nil interface

nodes.detail: A pointer type with a nil value
nodes.label: Typed nil

nodes.detail: Dynamic type exists, so x != nil
nodes.label: Boxed pointer

guides.practical: An interface holding a typed nil pointer still has a dynamic type. This commonly appears when a function returns an error interface from a typed pointer variable. Return a literal nil on the success path, and make nil-receiver behavior explicit for methods intended to support it.
guides.title: An interface carries a type and a value
guides.watchOut: An interface nil check does not prove that calling a method on the contained value is safe.

guides.caption: A type switch can handle nil, known types and a default case.

nodes.detail: The dynamic type is not yet known
nodes.label: Input

guides.practical: Use a type switch when an API intentionally accepts several unrelated kinds of values. Put the type-dependent behavior in a small boundary function, then pass concrete values into the rest of your code. A case listing multiple types leaves the case variable with the original interface type.
guides.title: Inspect a dynamic type once at the boundary
guides.watchOut: A type switch sees the exact dynamic type. A named string type is not the same case as string unless you handle it explicitly.

guides.caption: Embedding is composition with promoted selectors.

nodes.detail: The contained value is still there
nodes.label: Explicit path

guides.practical: Use embedding to expose a contained type deliberately, not to inherit an identity. The embedded value remains a field with its own receiver and state. A field or method on the outer type can hide a promoted selector; ambiguous promoted names must be reached through the explicit field path.
guides.title: Promotion makes fields and methods easier to reach
guides.watchOut: Outer is not assignable to Inner just because Inner is embedded in it. Promoted methods can nevertheless satisfy interfaces.

guides.caption: String returns text; it does not print or change the value.

nodes.detail: Uses the Stringer contract where applicable
nodes.label: Formatting

guides.practical: Keep String useful for logs and human-facing diagnostics. Some format verbs request a numeric or other specific representation, so not every fmt operation uses String. Separate machine serialization from String when a stable wire format is required.
guides.title: Formatting can ask the value how to display itself
guides.watchOut: Formatting the same value with a string verb from inside its own String method can recurse. Convert to the underlying type first.

guides.caption: any is an alias for interface{}; it is not a compile-time generic type parameter.

nodes.detail: Ask for a specific dynamic type
nodes.label: Recover type

guides.practical: Use any at a deliberately untyped boundary, such as decoding heterogeneous data. Prefer a concrete type when the caller and callee already agree on the shape. A checked type assertion reports failure without panic; an unchecked assertion is appropriate only when the contract guarantees the type.
guides.title: any preserves a dynamic value but promises no methods
guides.watchOut: Saying any accepts every type does not mean every operation is legal on the resulting interface value.

guides.caption: A constraint describes permitted types; a type argument selects one of them.

nodes.detail: T is checked at compile time
nodes.label: Generic function

guides.practical: Keep a type parameter connected to the values whose type relationship matters. The compiler often infers it from ordinary arguments, but explicit instantiation is available when inference has no evidence. Generic code may use only the operations guaranteed by its constraint.
guides.title: One algorithm keeps the caller’s element type
guides.watchOut: An any constraint does not permit arithmetic, ordering or arbitrary methods on T.

guides.caption: A type-set interface can be a constraint without being usable as an ordinary value type.

nodes.detail: Also allows named types based on int
nodes.label: Underlying member

nodes.detail: Allows ~int or ~float64; every member must support the operation
nodes.label: Union

guides.practical: Choose the smallest useful type set for the algorithm. Use cmp.Ordered for ordering and comparable when equality or map keys are needed. The tilde permits named types with the given underlying type. Constraints with type terms belong in type-parameter positions, not in ordinary variables.
guides.title: The type set controls the operations you may use
guides.watchOut: constraints is not a standard-library package. The experimental golang.org/x/exp/constraints package is a separate dependency.

guides.caption: Each instantiation keeps its element type through every operation.

nodes.detail: Design operations to accept nil storage
nodes.label: Zero value

guides.practical: A generic container should preserve the caller’s type and provide a clear empty-state contract. Return a value and a boolean when an element may be absent. Clearing removed pointer-bearing elements can avoid retaining objects through the backing slice after a pop.
guides.title: The receiver carries the container’s type argument
guides.watchOut: The zero value is useful only if the implementation supports it. Test an empty container before adding constructor requirements.

guides.caption: Go 1.27 adds method-specific type parameters.

nodes.detail: E is fixed by the receiver
nodes.label: Receiver type

nodes.detail: The mapping can change the element type
nodes.label: Result type

guides.practical: Keep the receiver’s parameter and the method’s parameter separate in your reasoning. A mapping function consumes E and produces F; a result container stores F. The caller can often infer F from the callback. This lesson uses the Go 1.27 toolchain bundled with GopherForge.
guides.title: A method can transform to a new element type
guides.watchOut: Interface methods cannot declare type parameters, and a generic method cannot implement an interface method.

guides.caption: A type parameter should express a relationship the ordinary signature cannot express as clearly.

nodes.detail: Best when one type is enough
nodes.label: Concrete type

guides.practical: Start with the required behavior and the result type. If the caller needs the same concrete element type back, generics can carry that relationship. If the function only invokes one method and returns no type-related result, a small interface often communicates the contract more directly.
guides.title: Choose the abstraction that preserves the needed relationship
guides.watchOut: Interface use does not guarantee a heap allocation, and generics do not guarantee faster code. Measure a real hot path first.

guides.caption: Wrapping links the new error to the old one instead of replacing its identity.

nodes.detail: Adds a message and an unwrap link
nodes.label: Context

guides.practical: Wrap where you can add useful operation context, and avoid repeating the same information at every layer. The percent-v verb formats an error as text; percent-w wraps it for later inspection. Wrapping exposes the cause as part of your API, so decide whether callers should be allowed to depend on it.
guides.title: Context can preserve the original cause
guides.watchOut: Only wrap a real non-nil error. A success path should return nil directly.

guides.caption: Inspect the error contract instead of parsing the human-readable message.

nodes.detail: Can a matching error type be extracted?
nodes.label: Type

guides.practical: Use Is for sentinel conditions that callers branch on and As for structured details such as a status or path. Both can traverse wrapped errors. Declare the destination variable for As first and pass its address; pointer error types require a pointer-valued destination variable.
guides.title: Identity and type answer different questions
guides.watchOut: Comparing Error() strings is brittle. Messages can change while the error identity and type remain stable.

guides.caption: All ordinary return paths pass through the registered cleanup.

nodes.detail: Cleanup is now tied to this function
nodes.label: Register

nodes.detail: Deferred cleanup runs before the caller continues
nodes.label: Exit

guides.practical: Register a close only after acquisition succeeds. Defer also runs during panic unwinding in the same goroutine. If closing can report a relevant failure, decide how that error participates in the result rather than discarding it by habit.
guides.title: Cleanup belongs next to successful acquisition
guides.watchOut: Calling os.Exit does not run deferred functions. A defer in a long loop also waits until the surrounding function exits.

guides.caption: The error interface is one method; behavior and metadata can live together.
guides.practical: Choose value or pointer receivers consistently with how the error will be returned and inspected. Keep Error free of side effects, because logging may call it more than once. An Unwrap method can expose a lower-level cause when that cause is part of the intended contract.
guides.title: An error can carry structured information
guides.watchOut: Avoid returning a typed nil pointer as an error interface; the resulting interface is non-nil.

guides.caption: Panic is an exceptional control flow, not a replacement for an error result.

nodes.detail: The caller decides how to handle it
nodes.label: Expected failure

nodes.detail: Stops normal execution in this goroutine
nodes.label: Broken invariant

guides.practical: Return errors for invalid input, missing files and canceled operations that callers can reasonably expect. Reserve panic for contracts that cannot continue safely, or for a deliberate internal boundary that will recover. An unrecovered panic terminates the program.
guides.title: Ordinary failures and broken invariants have different exits
guides.watchOut: A deferred recover in one goroutine cannot catch a panic that happens in another goroutine.

guides.caption: Recovery stops the unwind and lets the enclosing function return; it does not resume the panicking statement.

nodes.detail: A direct call in the deferred function catches it
nodes.label: Recover

guides.practical: Put recovery at a boundary that can decide what a failed operation means, such as handling one request. Convert the recovered failure into an explicit result and record enough context to diagnose the bug. Do not hide unexpected failures in an apparently successful zero result.
guides.title: Recover must run inside deferred cleanup
guides.watchOut: Calling recover through a non-deferred helper does not recover the panic. The recovering call must be made directly by the deferred function.

guides.caption: The import path locates the package; the package declaration names it in source.

nodes.detail: Package location below the module root
nodes.label: Directory

nodes.detail: Module path joined with that directory
nodes.label: Import

guides.practical: Keep the distinction between path and local name clear. A package may declare a name different from its directory, and an import alias can choose another local spelling. Import cycles are rejected, so arrange dependencies to flow from higher-level features toward shared lower-level packages.
guides.title: A package path comes from module plus directory
guides.watchOut: Moving a package directory changes its import path. Renaming only its package clause changes the name used by importing code.

guides.caption: Export is per identifier, including each struct field and method.

nodes.detail: Names beginning with uppercase are visible
nodes.label: Exported

nodes.detail: An exported type may still have private fields
nodes.label: Access

guides.practical: Give exported names useful documentation and keep implementation helpers private. Visibility applies between packages, not between files in the same package. Standard-library encoders such as encoding/json normally inspect exported struct fields, so field visibility also affects serialization.
guides.title: Capitalization marks the package boundary
guides.watchOut: An exported struct type does not automatically export its lowercase fields.

guides.caption: Production code and test code are compiled together according to the chosen test package.
guides.practical: Write tables around the observable contract: normal input, boundaries and failures. Use Fatal when continuing would make the rest of the test meaningless, and Error when collecting several independent mismatches is useful. Keep test data independent so adding a case does not change another case’s state.
guides.title: A test is ordinary Go with a testing entry point
guides.watchOut: Tests in package name_test exercise the exported API; tests in the same package can also inspect unexported details.

guides.caption: Read exported names with their package qualifier before deciding whether they are clear.

nodes.detail: The two words are read together
nodes.label: Public name

guides.practical: Prefer short, specific package names that describe the responsibility. Avoid repeating the package name in every exported identifier: cache.Store is usually clearer than cache.CacheStore. An import alias resolves a local naming conflict without changing the package’s own public name.
guides.title: The package name becomes part of every selector
guides.watchOut: A vague package name such as utils tends to gather unrelated responsibilities and makes the dependency direction harder to understand.

guides.caption: Within a package, variable dependency analysis also affects initialization order.
guides.practical: Prefer explicit constructors when configuration or failure handling belongs to the caller. Init functions take no arguments and return no result, which makes them a poor place for recoverable setup. Several init functions are allowed, but hidden dependence on file presentation order makes maintenance harder.
guides.title: Initialization follows dependencies before main
guides.watchOut: A goroutine started during init may continue running while later initialization proceeds. It needs explicit synchronization if ordering matters.

guides.caption: Completion of the exchange establishes synchronization between the participating goroutines.
guides.practical: Use an unbuffered channel when handing over a value should wait until a receiver is ready. Reason about both sides before launching work: a send performed before any receiver can run has nowhere to go. A channel communicates values and coordinates timing at the same time.
guides.title: A send and a receive meet at one point
guides.watchOut: Sending and then receiving on the same unbuffered channel in one goroutine blocks at the send.

guides.caption: A go statement does not provide an implicit join or keep main alive.

nodes.detail: Begins a goroutine; returns no handle
nodes.label: Start

guides.practical: Pick a completion contract before starting a goroutine. A closed channel can signal one operation’s completion; a WaitGroup can join several operations. Pass cancellation and result paths deliberately so a caller can stop and collect the work it starts.
guides.title: Starting work is separate from waiting for it
guides.watchOut: When main returns, the program exits even if other goroutines have unfinished work.

guides.caption: Close is a statement about the stream ending, not about discarding its queued values.
guides.practical: Give exactly one owner responsibility for closing. If multiple workers send, a coordinator can wait for all of them and close the results channel afterward. Receivers normally do not close because they cannot know that every sender has finished.
guides.title: The sender announces that no more values are coming
guides.watchOut: Sending to a closed channel or closing it twice panics. A channel used only for coordination does not always need to be closed.

guides.caption: If several cases can proceed, select chooses one; source order is not a priority rule.
guides.practical: Make every potentially blocking send or receive part of the cancellation design. A context is a signal, so the operation must actually observe it. When a channel may close, use the receive boolean to distinguish the end of the stream from a real zero-valued item.
guides.title: Wait for work and cancellation together
guides.watchOut: Cancellation does not forcibly stop a goroutine. Work that never checks ctx.Done can keep running.

guides.caption: Every access participating in the shared invariant must follow the same locking rule.

nodes.detail: Read and modify the protected state
nodes.label: Update

nodes.detail: Allow the next owner to enter
nodes.label: Leave

guides.practical: Keep the critical section short and make lock ownership easy to see. A deferred unlock protects early returns, while an explicit unlock may be clearer around a small block. Use a channel when transferring ownership expresses the operation better than protecting shared mutable state.
guides.title: One lock protects one shared invariant
guides.watchOut: Protect reads as well as writes. Copying a used mutex or taking the same mutex twice can break the synchronization contract.

guides.caption: A fixed worker count bounds concurrent processing, not the total number of jobs.

nodes.detail: Processes a job at a time
nodes.label: Worker A

guides.practical: Coordinate the full lifecycle: start workers, deliver jobs, close the jobs stream, wait for workers, then close the results stream. A separate results consumer may need to run while jobs are produced so backpressure cannot deadlock the producer.
guides.title: Bound the workers while letting jobs flow
guides.watchOut: Do not close results from an individual worker. Another worker may still be sending.

guides.caption: Buffering changes when a send blocks; it does not remove synchronization requirements.

nodes.detail: Two sends may queue without receivers
nodes.label: Space available

guides.practical: Choose capacity to express the intended amount of queued work. A small buffer can smooth bursts and decouple short timing differences. It cannot fix a missing receiver or an endless producer; once capacity is exhausted, backpressure still reaches the sender.
guides.title: A channel buffer has a finite number of slots
guides.watchOut: len(ch) is a momentary queue size, not a reliable precondition for a future send or receive.

guides.caption: A closed channel may still contain unread values.

nodes.detail: Ends after the buffer is empty
nodes.label: Drain and stop

guides.practical: Use range when the entire stream should be consumed until its producer finishes. If cancellation is also required, use a select loop and inspect the two-result receive. Assign close ownership to the producer or the coordinator that knows all producers are done.
guides.title: The receiver drains before the loop ends
guides.watchOut: Ranging over a nil channel blocks forever. A never-closed stream also never ends by itself.

guides.caption: Default changes a blocking select into a try operation.

nodes.detail: Wait until a case can proceed
nodes.label: Blocking alternative

guides.practical: Use a default case when a skipped operation is part of the contract, such as a best-effort status update. A loop with default can spin continuously when no work is ready. Prefer a blocking select with cancellation or an explicit timing source for a waiting loop.
guides.title: Default means continue immediately when nothing is ready
guides.watchOut: Default does not run after a timeout and does not wait briefly. It is selected immediately when no communication is ready.

guides.caption: A bidirectional channel can be passed to a directional parameter.
guides.practical: Use direction in function signatures to communicate roles and let the compiler reject accidental reverse operations. The owner still needs a runtime lifecycle rule: a send-only parameter can close a channel, but that ability does not establish that it is the correct owner to do so.
guides.title: The type limits who may send or receive
guides.watchOut: Direction is a permission, not an ownership guarantee. Two senders can still race to close unless the design assigns one closer.

guides.caption: Do does not return to any caller until the one initialization call has finished.

nodes.detail: The first caller runs the function
nodes.label: One shared Once

nodes.detail: Waits if initialization is in progress
nodes.label: Caller A

guides.practical: Keep the Once next to the state it protects, and keep that state in one shared object. It is suitable for initialization that must run at most once. Use another design if an operation may fail and needs retries; Once records the attempt rather than guaranteeing successful initialization.
guides.title: Concurrent callers share one completed initialization
guides.watchOut: If the function panics, Once still considers it done. Calling Do recursively on that same Once deadlocks.

guides.caption: The same operation can use files, memory buffers or other implementations.
guides.practical: Accept interfaces that describe only the I/O behavior the function uses. A reader may return bytes and an error in the same call; process those bytes before the error. Standard helpers such as io.Copy and io.ReadAll handle the protocol details, but ReadAll uses memory proportional to the input.
guides.title: Separate the operation from the transport
guides.watchOut: Do not assume one Read fills the requested buffer. For an exact byte count, use io.ReadFull.

guides.caption: Decoding into an existing value can preserve fields absent from the input.
guides.practical: Treat tags as part of the external contract and test representative encoded values. Decode into a fresh struct when missing fields should become zero. Use a pointer field when an absent field must be distinguished from a present zero, and consider DisallowUnknownFields for strict input.
guides.title: Exported fields and tags define the wire representation
guides.watchOut: Do not silently ignore Marshal or Unmarshal errors. Lowercase fields remain invisible even if they carry a json tag.

guides.caption: A Duration is an int64 measured in nanoseconds.

nodes.detail: A plain number has no readable unit
nodes.label: Quantity

guides.practical: Use Add and Sub for instants and Before, After or Equal for comparisons. Time values may contain location and monotonic information, so == can differ from Equal. A context timeout or timer is often more useful than Sleep when the operation must be cancelable.
guides.title: Make units visible in every duration
guides.watchOut: time.Sleep(5) requests five nanoseconds; scheduling overhead determines when execution actually resumes.

guides.caption: slices.SortFunc takes a three-way comparison, not a less-than boolean.
guides.practical: Make the comparison consistent and transitive so the sorting algorithm can rely on it. Sorting changes the supplied slice in place; clone first if callers need the original order. Use SortStableFunc when equal elements must retain their original relative order.
guides.title: Compare the first key, then break ties with the second
guides.watchOut: Subtracting integers as a comparator can overflow. cmp.Compare expresses the ordering without that overflow risk.

guides.caption: The context carries a cancellation signal; it does not interrupt work automatically.
guides.practical: Pass context as the first parameter and propagate it to operations that already accept one. Call the returned cancel function to release resources, even if the deadline eventually expires. Keep contexts out of long-lived structs unless an API explicitly requires that lifetime.
guides.title: Cancellation has to reach the blocking operation
guides.watchOut: Do not use context values for optional arguments or general application state. Values are for request-scoped data crossing API boundaries.

guides.caption: The lesson tests real handler behavior with an in-memory transport.

nodes.detail: Writes status, headers and body into the recorder
nodes.label: Handler

guides.practical: Keep HTTP behavior separate from business logic so handler tests can check methods, paths and invalid input directly. Set headers and status before writing a body; the first Write otherwise commits status 200. In GopherForge’s Wasm sandbox, httptest is the supported way to exercise these routes.
guides.title: A handler can be exercised without opening a socket
guides.watchOut: Passing an in-memory handler test does not claim that the Wasm program can bind a network socket.

guides.caption: strconv parses representations; a numeric type conversion does not parse a string.

nodes.detail: May contain invalid or out-of-range data
nodes.label: Text input

nodes.detail: Use only after the error decision
nodes.label: Typed result

guides.practical: Use ParseInt with an explicit base and bit size when the data format requires a specific integer representation. Atoi targets int, whose width depends on the architecture. Distinguish syntax errors from out-of-range values when the user needs a useful message.
guides.title: Text parsing returns a value and a failure path
guides.watchOut: Whitespace is not automatically trimmed by Atoi. Decide whether your input contract allows it and normalize explicitly.

guides.caption: An image.Image is a pixel interface, not a filename or encoded data blob.
guides.practical: Read Bounds rather than assuming every image starts at (0,0). Image implementations may be views over shared pixel storage. Rendering and encoding are separate steps: the app can display a PNG written by a program, while the Go program still uses the standard image and encoding interfaces.
guides.title: Pixels and encoded files are separate representations
guides.watchOut: A rectangle excludes Max. Iterate while x < bounds.Max.X and y < bounds.Max.Y.

bugs.brief: This should print the doubled value. It does not compile.
bugs.explanation: `doubled` is declared and never used, which is a compile error in Go rather than a warning. The language treats an unused local as a mistake you meant to catch — either print it or do not declare it.

bugs.brief: This should count words. It panics at run time.
bugs.explanation: A `var` map is nil. Reading from a nil map is fine and gives the zero value, which is why the loop looks safe — but writing to one panics. It needed `make(map[string]int)`.

bugs.brief: This should add an item to the caller's slice. The caller never sees it.
bugs.explanation: append returns a new slice header, and the parameter is a copy of the caller's. Assigning to it changes nothing outside the function. The signature has to return the slice, or take a pointer to it.

bugs.brief: This should fail loudly when the file is missing. It carries on instead.
bugs.explanation: The error is discarded with `_`, so a missing file returns an empty slice that looks exactly like an empty file. In Go an error is a value you have to decide about; throwing it away is the decision to pretend nothing went wrong.

bugs.brief: This should recognise a missing file. It stops recognising it the moment anybody wraps the error.
bugs.explanation: `==` compares the error you were handed, not the chain inside it. One `%w` between you and the sentinel and the branch stops firing. `errors.Is(err, os.ErrNotExist)` walks the chain, which is what it is for.

bugs.brief: This compiles and runs. `go vet` and every reviewer will still stop on it.
bugs.explanation: Error strings are lower case and unpunctuated, because they get wrapped: yours ends up in the middle of a longer sentence, and a capital letter there reads as a new one starting.

bugs.brief: This should close each file as it finishes with it. It holds every one of them open instead.
bugs.explanation: A defer runs when the *function* returns, not when the loop body ends. Over a long list that is every file open at once. The body has to become its own function, or the close has to be called explicitly.

bugs.brief: This should hand three jobs to a worker. It panics somewhere in the middle.
bugs.explanation: The receiver closes the channel. Closing means "no more values are coming", which only the sender knows — and the next send lands on a closed channel and panics. The sender closes, after its last send.

bugs.brief: This should wait for three workers. It sometimes returns before any of them have run.
bugs.explanation: Add runs inside the goroutine, so Wait can be reached while the counter is still zero and return immediately. Add belongs before `go`, on the line that decides there will be another worker.

bugs.explanation: A context.Context is the first parameter, always, and it is named ctx. It is a convention rather than a rule, which is exactly why breaking it is noticed: every other function in the codebase reads the other way round.

answerPoints: Every type has a zero value and every declaration produces it: 0, "", false, nil for pointers, slices, maps, channels and interfaces, and a struct whose fields are each their own zero.

Every declaration is initialized, but allowed operations still depend on the type: append works on a nil slice, assigning a nil map panics, and a nil-channel send blocks. Types that require configuration must make that requirement explicit.

The exchange is that the zero value has to be designed. sync.Mutex and bytes.Buffer are usable at zero; a type that needs setup has to say so, which is why NewThing exists as a convention rather than a language feature.
interviews.prompt: Go has no constructors and no uninitialised memory. What is a zero value, and what does the language get in exchange for insisting on one?
interviews.trap: Saying it is "like default initialisation in C++ or Java". Those languages leave some things uninitialised or require a constructor to run; Go's point is that neither is ever true.

answerPoints: When the method mutates the receiver, because a value receiver mutates a copy and the caller sees nothing.
When the value is large enough that copying it per call matters — though that is a measurement, not a guess.

Prefer a consistent receiver convention when a type needs mutation or must not be copied. This is design guidance, not a language rule: T and *T have different method sets, and some mixed receiver APIs can be deliberate.
interviews.prompt: When do you give a method a pointer receiver rather than a value receiver?
interviews.trap: "Pointers are faster." For a small struct a copy is often cheaper than the indirection, and the real reason is mutation, not speed.

answerPoints: A slice is a pointer to an array, a length and a capacity. Length is how many elements you can index; capacity is how many the underlying array has from that pointer onwards.
append writes in place while length is below capacity. When it is not, it allocates a bigger array, copies, and returns a slice pointing at the new one.
That is why the return value of append must be used: after a growth the old slice header is stale.
interviews.prompt: What is the difference between a slice's length and its capacity, and when does append allocate?
interviews.trap: Saying append "always allocates" or "never does". Which one happened is invisible from the call site, which is exactly why the result has to be assigned.

answerPoints: left has room in the shared array, so append writes index 2 in place rather than allocating.
right[2] is that same element, so it now reads 99 — nothing was copied and nothing warned you.
Cutting the capacity with a three-index slice, base[0:2:2], makes the append allocate instead and breaks the aliasing on purpose.
interviews.code:
base := make([]int, 3, 8)
left := base[0:2]
right := base[0:3]
left = append(left, 99)
interviews.prompt: Two slices are taken from the same array. What happens to the second when you append to the first?
interviews.trap: Assuming a slice expression copies. It never does: it makes another view of the same array.

answerPoints: Structurally and implicitly: a type satisfies an interface by having the methods, with no declaration that it intends to.
It is checked at compile time, at the point of assignment or call — not at run time, and not where the type is defined.

So an interface can be declared by the consumer, next to the code that needs it, and existing types satisfy it without being touched. That is why Go interfaces are usually small and defined where they are used.
interviews.prompt: How does a type come to satisfy an interface in Go, and when is that decided?
interviews.trap: Reaching for "duck typing". The checking is static; nothing is discovered at run time.

answerPoints: An interface value is a pair: a type and a value. It is nil only when both halves are.
Returning a nil *NotFoundError as an error fills the type half, so the interface is not nil even though the pointer is.
The fix is to return a literal nil rather than a typed nil variable — and to not declare a typed error variable for the happy path in the first place.
interviews.prompt: A function returns an error that is not nil, but the pointer inside it is. How does that happen?
interviews.trap: "err == nil should be true because err is nil." It is the most reliably surprising thing in the language, and the answer is that the comparison is about the pair.

answerPoints: Wrap with %w when you are adding context the caller does not have — which file, which key, which request — and the original still matters for a decision further up.
Return it unchanged when you have nothing to add. A wrap that says "failed to read: failed to read: no such file" is noise.
Do not wrap when the original is an implementation detail you do not want callers matching on: that turns a private failure into part of your API.
interviews.prompt: When do you wrap an error, and when do you return it as it is?
interviews.trap: Wrapping everything by reflex. Every %w is a promise that callers may use errors.Is against what is inside.

answerPoints: errors.Is asks whether an error in the chain is a particular value — a sentinel such as io.EOF or os.ErrNotExist.
errors.As asks whether an error in the chain is a particular type, and if so assigns it to your variable so you can read its fields.
Both walk the wrap chain, which is why == fails on a wrapped error and errors.Is does not.
interviews.prompt: What is the difference between errors.Is and errors.As?
interviews.trap: Comparing with == out of habit. It works right up until somebody adds a %w between you and the sentinel.

answerPoints: go.mod records the module path and the minimum version your build needs. Go picks the highest minimum across the whole graph — minimal version selection — so a build is reproducible without a lock file.
go.sum records a cryptographic hash of each module's content, so a version that changed underneath you fails verification instead of building.
They answer different questions: go.mod is which version, go.sum is whether the bytes are the ones everybody else got.
interviews.prompt: What does a require line in go.mod pin, and what does go.sum add on top of it?
interviews.trap: Calling go.sum a lock file. It does not choose versions; it verifies whatever was chosen.

answerPoints: The sender closes, because closing means "no more values are coming" and only the sending side knows that.
A receiver that closes can race with a send in flight, and a send on a closed channel panics — it is not an error you can handle at the send.
With several senders, nobody closes directly: a WaitGroup waits for them and one goroutine closes afterwards.
interviews.prompt: Who closes a channel, and what goes wrong when the other side does it?
interviews.trap: "Whoever finishes first closes it." Closing is not cleanup; it is a message, and it can only be sent by the side that has the news.

answerPoints: A mutex protects state several goroutines share: a counter, a cache, a map. The value stays where it is and access is serialised.
A channel hands a value over: one goroutine is finished with it and another should have it. Ownership moves.
If routing something through a channel would just be ceremony around an increment, it is a mutex. If two goroutines are passing work along, it is a channel.
interviews.prompt: Mutex or channel — how do you choose?
interviews.trap: "Share memory by communicating, so always use a channel." The proverb is advice about design, not a ban on sync — the standard library is full of mutexes.

answerPoints: A goroutine blocked on a channel nobody will ever send to, or on a receive from a context that is never cancelled. It is not an error anywhere: it simply stops, holding its stack.
It shows as memory that climbs and never comes back, and as a goroutine count that only goes up — runtime.NumGoroutine, or the goroutine profile from net/http/pprof.

The fixes are structural: give every goroutine a way to be told to stop, usually a context, and make sure every channel it might block on either gets closed or gets a select with a cancellation branch.
interviews.prompt: What is a goroutine leak, and how would you notice one in production?
interviews.trap: Expecting the runtime to complain. It only reports a deadlock when *every* goroutine is asleep — one stuck goroutine beside a busy program is silent.

answerPoints: Its Done channel is closed. That is the whole mechanism — cancellation is a closed channel, which is why a select can wait on it and why it can be observed by any number of goroutines at once.
Cancellation propagates down to contexts derived from it, never up.
Nothing is stopped for you. A goroutine that never checks Done keeps running; the context only makes it possible to notice.
interviews.prompt: What actually happens when you cancel a context?
interviews.trap: Believing cancel() kills anything. Go has no way to stop another goroutine — cancellation is a request that has to be read.

answerPoints: A Read may return data and an error in the same call — n bytes were genuinely read even if err is io.EOF.
So the caller processes the first n bytes before looking at err, in that order. Checking the error first and returning loses data.
io.EOF is not a failure: it is how a reader says it has finished. Any other error is.
interviews.prompt: io.Reader returns (n int, err error). Why both, and what must a caller do with them?
interviews.trap: Treating a non-nil error as "nothing was read". That is true of most APIs and not of this one, which is why the interface is worth asking about.

questions.explanation: Short declaration is function-scoped. At package level you must write var count = 0.
options: Only inside a for or if statement
questions.prompt: Where can this line appear?

questions.explanation: An unused local is an error in Go, not a warning. Unused imports are the same. There is no flag to soften it.
options: A warning about an unused variable
cannot use host as type string
questions.prompt: What does the compiler say?

questions.explanation: Every Go value starts at its zero value. For a string that is "", for a pointer nil, for an int 0. There is no uninitialised memory.
options: A compile error — it needs a value
questions.prompt: What is the value of s?

questions.explanation: Ordinary Go failures are returned as error values. A fallible function returns an error beside its result, and the caller decides what to do about it.
options: To avoid exceptions: failure is a value you must handle
The second value is always ignored
questions.prompt: Why does Go return two values here?

questions.explanation: Same rule as an unused variable: it is an error. If you need the import only for its side effects, write _ "os".
options: A warning, but it still builds
questions.prompt: The file imports "os" but never mentions os again. What happens?

questions.explanation: The names in the result list are variables. A return with no arguments sends those. The Tour says keep that for short functions.
options: A compile error — return needs values
Whatever is in scope named x, y
The named results as they stand
questions.prompt: What does a naked return send?

questions.explanation: A keyed literal names the fields it supplies, so adding a field does not change those names. Omitted fields take their zero values. A positional literal must supply every field in declaration order.
options: It is the only form vet accepts
It survives a field being added
Positional literals can leave any fields out
questions.prompt: Why is the named form preferred for a struct literal?

questions.explanation: A value receiver is a copy. The method compiles, runs and mutates the copy, and nothing warns you that the change went nowhere.
questions.prompt: Grow has a value receiver and increments a field. What does the caller see?

questions.code: type Point struct{ X, Y int }
questions.explanation: A struct is never nil. Its zero value has every field at that field's own zero, and the variable is usable straight away.
options: A struct with X and Y at 0
questions.prompt: What is `var p Point` before anything is assigned to it?

questions.explanation: Escape analysis notices the value outlives the call and allocates it where it survives. This is ordinary Go — every New... does it.
options: A dangling pointer at run time
It works only for small types
questions.prompt: A function returns the address of a local variable. What happens?

questions.explanation: A closure captures the variable, not its value, so writes made through one are visible through the other.
questions.prompt: What do two closures over the same variable share?

questions.explanation: Reslicing does not copy. b shares a's backing array, so writing through b writes through a — until an append outgrows cap.
questions.prompt: What does this print?

questions.explanation: Inside cap it writes in place and the sharing stays. Past cap it allocates a new array, and the two slices quietly stop being connected.
options: Never — append always writes in place
When the result would exceed cap(b)
questions.prompt: When does append stop writing into the original array?

questions.explanation: Reading a missing key gives the zero value. Use the two-value form, n, ok := scores["nope"], when absent and zero mean different things.
options: The zero value for the map's type
questions.prompt: The map has no key "nope". What does this give?

questions.explanation: len counts bytes. é is two bytes in UTF-8. Range over the string, or convert to []rune, to count characters.
questions.prompt: What is len("héllo")?

questions.explanation: i is a byte offset, so it jumps by more than one for multi-byte characters. r is the rune itself.
options: The byte offset of the character
Always the same as the loop count
questions.prompt: In for i, r := range s, what is i?

questions.explanation: The length is in the type. The Tour's Arrays page is the one people skip, then a [32]byte parameter refuses a [16]byte.
options: Arrays cannot be passed to functions
questions.prompt: Why will this not compile?

questions.code: double := func(n int) int { return n * 2 }
questions.explanation: The Tour: functions are values. The type includes the arguments and the result. func(int) int is not the same as func(int) string.
questions.prompt: What is the type of this value?

questions.code:
type Adder interface{ Add() }
func (c *Counter) Add() { c.n++ }
questions.explanation: A pointer receiver puts the method in *Counter's method set only. A value receiver would put it in both.
questions.prompt: Add is declared on *Counter. Which type satisfies Adder?

questions.explanation: An interface is nil only when both its type and its value are. Return a bare nil rather than a typed nil pointer.
options: The interface holds a type and a value; only the value is nil
Because MyError does not implement error
It does not — this prints nothing
questions.prompt: Why does this print "not nil"?

questions.explanation: io.Reader is one method, and half the standard library accepts it. The larger the interface, the fewer things can be passed to you.
options: One with five methods, so it is complete
questions.prompt: Which interface is easier for callers to satisfy?

questions.explanation: The consumer knows what it needs. Declaring it there keeps the interface as small as the use, and implementers need not import anything.
options: In the package that consumes it
In the package that implements it
questions.prompt: Where should an interface usually be declared?

questions.explanation: The Tour's Stringers page: fmt.Stringer is String() string. Nothing registers. Do not Sprint the value from its own String.
options: A String() keyword on the type
A String() method; fmt looks for it
questions.prompt: How does fmt print a type as a dotted IP?

questions.explanation: ~float64 means any type whose underlying type is float64, so `type Celsius float64` is admitted. Without it, only float64 itself is.
questions.prompt: What does the ~ add to a constraint?

questions.code:
func A[T any](v T)
func B(v interface{})
questions.explanation: A gets the caller's actual type, so its result stays typed and mistakes are compile errors. B gets a value the caller must assert out of.
options: B is checked at compile time
questions.prompt: How does `any` as a constraint differ from interface{} as a parameter?

questions.explanation: Methods repeat the type's parameters but cannot add new ones, which is why Map is a function in every Go library and a method in none.
options: Only if the receiver is a value
No; it must be a function
questions.prompt: Can a method introduce a type parameter of its own?

questions.explanation: T might be a string or an int, for which nil is not a value, and T{} is not valid for every type. A declared variable is the zero of whatever T turned out to be.
options: var zero T; return zero, false
questions.prompt: How do you return the zero value of a type parameter T?

questions.explanation: Nothing here needs the concrete type: no container to keep typed, no operator, no second type. The plain interface parameter says the same thing and reads once instead of twice.
options: Take the interface as a parameter
questions.prompt: The constraint is an interface with one method and nothing else. Now what?

questions.explanation: %w wraps: errors.Is and errors.As can still see through it. %v formats it into a string and the original is gone.
questions.prompt: Which keeps the original error reachable?

questions.explanation: errors.Is unwraps. A direct == fails the moment anyone adds context with %w, and comparing strings breaks on a reworded message.
questions.prompt: How should a caller test for a known error?

questions.explanation: Function scope, not block scope, and it runs on a panic too. That is what makes it the right place for cleanup.
options: At the end of the enclosing block
When the function returns, however it returns
Only on a normal return, not on a panic
questions.prompt: When does the deferred call run?

questions.explanation: On failure Atoi returns 0 and an error. Discarding the error turns bad input into a plausible-looking zero, which is the hardest bug to find.
options: Nothing, if you are sure input is a number
questions.prompt: What is wrong with this?

questions.explanation: recover is nil unless it is called from a function deferred on the panicking goroutine. A named result is how the error gets out.
options: On the next line after panic
questions.prompt: Where does recover actually work?

questions.explanation: An unbuffered channel is a rendezvous: the send waits for a receiver, and the only goroutine that could receive is the one sending.
options: fatal error: all goroutines are asleep - deadlock!
It blocks forever with no message
questions.prompt: What happens when this runs?

questions.explanation: Closing tells receivers there is no more. A receiver cannot know that, and closing twice — or sending after a close — panics.
options: The receiver, when it has had enough
questions.prompt: Who should close a channel?

questions.explanation: With a default, select never blocks. Without one, it waits for the first branch that becomes ready.
options: Runs when every other case is ready
Makes select return at once when nothing is ready
Repeats the select until a case fires
questions.prompt: What does a default case do in a select?

questions.explanation: Add inside the goroutine races with Wait, which may see a counter of zero and return before anything started.
options: After the loop, once, with the total
questions.prompt: Where does wg.Add(1) belong?

questions.explanation: A goroutine blocked on a channel nobody reads is a leak: it holds its stack and everything it references, for the life of the program.
options: It blocks on the send forever and is never collected
The send fails with an error
questions.prompt: The receiver returned early. What happens to this goroutine?

questions.explanation: First parameter, never stored. A stored context outlives the call it belonged to, and cancelling it then means nothing.
options: Stored in the struct that needs it
As the first parameter, named ctx
questions.prompt: Where does a context belong?

questions.explanation: The Tour: sends block when the buffer is full, receives when it is empty. A buffer of 1 is a mailbox of one, not a queue without a lid.
options: When the one slot is already full
Always — a buffer is only a hint
questions.prompt: When does a send on make(chan int, 1) block?

questions.explanation: Do runs f once for that Once, even across goroutines. A different f on the second call is ignored. Do not copy the Once after first use.
options: Runs a new function if you pass one
questions.prompt: What does once.Do(f) do on the second call?

questions.explanation: A directory is a package. Every file in it shares one package clause, and two different clauses in one directory is an error.
questions.prompt: What decides which package a file belongs to?

questions.explanation: internal/ is enforced by the compiler: only code rooted at its parent may import it. It is how a module keeps an implementation private.
options: Only the package that declares it
questions.prompt: Who can import example.com/app/internal/store?

questions.explanation: Case is the visibility rule. Message is exported, message is not, and there is no third level.
questions.prompt: What makes an identifier visible outside its package?

questions.explanation: The module path prefixes every import inside it: the directory greet becomes example.com/app/greet.
options: It must be a real URL that resolves
It is the prefix every package in the module is imported by
questions.prompt: What is the module path in go.mod for?

questions.explanation: Read, and nothing else. That is why a file, a network connection and a string can all be passed to the same function.
questions.prompt: How many methods does io.Reader have?

questions.explanation: Go passes everything by value. Without the pointer, Unmarshal would fill a copy and the caller would see nothing change.
options: So it can fill a value the caller owns
Because JSON is always an object
It does not — that & is optional
questions.prompt: Why does Unmarshal take a pointer?

questions.explanation: Each case reports separately, so one failure does not hide the rest, and -run can select a single case by name.
options: A subtest that can fail on its own and be run by name
questions.prompt: What does t.Run give you?

questions.explanation: Scan returns false for both EOF and failure. Err() afterwards is the only thing that tells them apart.
options: Scan returns false only at EOF
questions.prompt: The loop ended. How do you know it was not an error?

questions.explanation: ServeHTTP(ResponseWriter, *Request). HandlerFunc turns a function into that type. httptest exercises it without a listen.
questions.prompt: How many methods does http.Handler have?

questions.explanation: The Tour's Errors page uses Atoi for this: failure is a value. Ignoring the error turns "x" into a plausible zero.
questions.prompt: What does strconv.Atoi("x") return?
