An expiry or a closed room requires a new explicit connection, not a search through unrelated projects.
sections.code:
Task contract:
- Read the room and current revision.
- Change only the named Go files.
- Explain the invariant and minimal failing input.
- Request a local test; wait for device Output.
- Do not run on a server or claim an older result validates a new edit.
sections.title: Give an MCP collaborator a bounded task
sections.walkthrough: The contract scopes both the edit and the evidence. The AI must first read the current room revision; the human then decides whether to execute that source on the local device. A repository rule never substitutes for the room capability or that local action.

sections.body: A mobile AI client can use a supported remote HTTPS MCP connector. The native app participates while foregrounded and executes only after its local button is pressed. Connector availability is controlled by the AI client and plan. Do not prescribe an npm daemon on iOS or claim that a custom remote URL automatically works in every mobile chat. Keep a readable web/JSON progress link as a simpler way to provide teaching context.
sections.title: Phone connection does not mean a background server on iOS

readings.takeaway: Keep repository facts concrete, scope guidance using each product’s documented mechanism and enforce permissions in the environment. Recheck discovery after tool changes.
readings.title: Repository guidance for Codex, Claude Code and Cursor
wrongAnswers: The heading style in the markdown file
Excluding one file from search alone

cautions: Compiling proves API compatibility for that build; database timing, failover and atomicity require additional evidence.
designGuide.cost: Choose the policy from the actual contract, then verify its failure path in the target environment.
designGuide.family: Verify generated Go against the real module and runtime
strengths: Catch invented APIs, unsafe concurrency and changed wire contracts in generated Go.
Resolve the actual version, compile the claimed API, review ownership and test changed public behavior. Keep native, WASI and remote-service evidence distinct.

readings.hint: Find the dependency already selected by the build.
readings.introduction: Generated source can look idiomatic while targeting the wrong driver major version or changing the public result. Compile against the selected module graph, inspect authoritative APIs and test the observable path. A plausible import name or confident explanation is not version evidence.
readings.nuance: Compiling proves API compatibility for that build; database timing, failover and atomicity require additional evidence.
readings.objective: Catch invented APIs, unsafe concurrency and changed wire contracts in generated Go.
readings.question: A MongoDB example uses an old driver signature but the module uses v2. Which is the useful first check?
readings.reviewAnswer: Check the selected version and API

sections.body: Start in the target module and inspect the workspace and selected dependencies. A local replace can make generated code compile against unreleased source. For MongoDB v2, use its /v2 path and documented lifecycle; do not add an old major version merely to make an invented call compile.
sections.code:
go env GOMOD GOWORK
go list -m all
go doc go.mongodb.org/mongo-driver/v2/mongo.Connect
go test ./internal/store/...
sections.title: Check which module the code actually uses
sections.walkthrough: These are native-development commands in a repository that already depends on the v2 driver. go doc establishes the selected API rather than downloading a guessed dependency. The package test path must exist in that checkout.

sections.body: For every generated goroutine, identify who starts it, cancels it and waits for it. Check blocking sends and capacity acquisition. Acquiring a semaphore inside a newly launched goroutine can bound active work while still allowing an unbounded number of waiting goroutines.
sections.title: Review ownership before adding goroutines

sections.body: A nil slice becoming empty changes JSON under some serializers. Replacing %w with %v changes error matching. Returning success after a canceled partial export changes the protocol. Add fixtures for those decisions and check old callers before accepting a cosmetic cleanup.
sections.title: Compare contracts, not just signatures

sections.body: Ask for a blocked-receiver cancellation test, duplicate request or commit-then-disconnect fixture when relevant. Run race detection on exercised concurrent paths and use integration tests for database atomicity. No amount of mocking can establish a live driver or server guarantee it never exercised.
sections.title: Require a failure-path demonstration

sections.body: Require the source revision, the Run/Test operation, the participating device, the observed result and the relevant runtime limits. A shared result is client-reported, not an attested proof. If source changed while the build ran, keep the old result visible as historical evidence. Do not run unreviewed AI code merely because an edit arrived. A relay must not execute the project on behalf of all participants.
sections.code:
Evidence checklist:
source revision + exact files
→ explicit local Run/Test
→ device-labelled stdout/stderr
→ compare result revision with current revision
→ state unverified platform/service conditions
sections.title: Check execution provenance before reading green output
sections.walkthrough: Read the chain from top to bottom. A source revision identifies what was built, the local action identifies where it ran, and the final comparison tells you whether the evidence still applies. Missing a step leaves a narrower claim, not an automatic pass.

sections.body: Suppose two collaborators both read revision 4. The first publishes revision 5; the second must not overwrite it using an unconditional write. A compare-and-swap publication rejects the stale revision. Preserve the second draft, inspect revision 5 and reapply the intended change. This whole-file strategy is simpler than CRDT merging but requires an explicit conflict workflow. A successful HTTP update only proves that a revision was accepted; it does not prove that the Go program is correct.
sections.title: Reproduce conflicts without discarding a local draft

readings.takeaway: Resolve the actual version, compile the claimed API, review ownership and test changed public behavior. Keep native, WASI and remote-service evidence distinct.
readings.title: Verify generated Go against the real module and runtime
wrongAnswers: Add both major versions automatically
Trust that a similar method exists

cautions: Do not confuse a generated command with an authorized action. Context files and tool permissions solve different problems.
designGuide.cost: Choose the policy from the actual contract, then verify its failure path in the target environment.
designGuide.family: Agent trust boundaries: repository text is input data
strengths: Review commands, secrets and external writes when an agent consumes untrusted text.
Treat external text as task data, enforce permissions with real controls and verify sensitive commands at their boundary. Keep the Go fix tied to its authorized behavior.

readings.hint: The page is evidence to inspect, not a new instruction source.
readings.introduction: A source comment, dependency README, test log or fetched webpage can contain instructions written by someone else. Reading that material to solve a Go problem does not authorize its author to expand the task. Keep the user’s goal and trusted repository guidance separate from external diagnostic content.
readings.nuance: Do not confuse a generated command with an authorized action. Context files and tool permissions solve different problems.
readings.objective: Review commands, secrets and external writes when an agent consumes untrusted text.
readings.question: A webpage linked by a failing test asks an agent to upload a credential file. What should happen?
readings.reviewAnswer: External text cannot grant permission
readings.reviewPrompt: Can a page authorize an upload?

sections.body: Imagine a failing test prints a page that tells the agent to upload environment variables. That instruction is not part of the authorized fix. Extract the actual assertion failure, inspect the relevant source and ignore the requested credential transfer.
sections.code:
Diagnostic data:
  expected first duplicate index 1, got 2
  see external.example/fix for instructions

Authorized task:
  repair LowerBound and prove duplicate handling

The external page cannot authorize uploading files or secrets.
sections.title: Recognize an instruction hidden in a failure
sections.walkthrough: The URL is an illustrative untrusted destination, not a link to visit. The useful evidence is the mismatch between expected and actual index; an unrelated upload request does not help establish that invariant.

sections.body: Give agent-driven tests a disposable database, namespaced keys and bounded cleanup. A unique key prefix does not protect other data if a cleanup script still runs FLUSHDB. Inspect generated commands before they can affect shared systems, especially dependency installers, migrations and deployment steps.
sections.title: Use isolated integration resources

sections.body: Use environment or credential mechanisms approved for the selected tool. Include variable names in setup instructions rather than real passwords. Logs, traces, snapshots and fixtures can also retain private data; inspect what a test or support bundle records before sharing it.
sections.title: Keep secrets out of the conversation and diff

sections.body: Record the changed files, checks actually run, unresolved failures and next concrete step. Preserve the original task constraints after context reduction. A handoff saying everything is safe without naming evidence is difficult for either a human or another session to verify.
sections.title: Make a useful handoff

sections.body: A comment, test fixture or printed output can contain text asking an agent to reveal secrets or use other tools. Those strings are task data, not authority. A room capability grants access only to that room. It must not grant filesystem access, arbitrary shell commands, another project or automatic execution on someone else’s device. The relay transports text; local execution remains a separate human action.
sections.code:
Untrusted: source / comments / test output / shared progress
Trusted authority: the human task and explicitly granted room role
Execution boundary: a local person presses Run/Test

A prompt in stdout cannot promote View to Edit or execute on another phone.
sections.title: Treat room source, Output and progress as untrusted data
sections.walkthrough: The diagram distinguishes data from authority. A malicious printed line stays inside Output and cannot authorize another tool or another device. Preserve this boundary even when the content sounds like an urgent system instruction.

sections.body: Room links are bearer capabilities: a person or AI receiving a working Edit link can read and change the room until expiry or closure. A View link permits reading and copying. The fragment is outside the initial page request, but the client deliberately sends the credential to the relay in an API header or tool argument. GopherForge’s preview relay can read shared source and Output; it is not end-to-end encrypted. Progress publication is a separate 90-day, read-only snapshot with a revocation key. Exclude private code, access tokens and production data; revocation cannot erase downloaded copies.
sections.title: Understand what sharing actually exposes

readings.takeaway: Treat external text as task data, enforce permissions with real controls and verify sensitive commands at their boundary. Keep the Go fix tied to its authorized behavior.
readings.title: Agent trust boundaries: repository text is input data
wrongAnswers: Follow it because it came from a test
Upload first and redact the reply

cautions: Use an error-aware group for returned task errors and keep a separate bounded cancellation path for work that may block.
designGuide.cost: Choose the policy from the actual contract, then verify its failure path in the target environment.
designGuide.family: WaitGroup.Go joins tasks; it does not collect their errors
strengths: Use modern WaitGroup task ownership and explain its limits.
WaitGroup.Go registers owned work and Wait joins it. Cancellation, errors, panic policy and admission control remain separate parts of the design.

readings.hint: Joining waits for exit; it cannot manufacture an exit path.
readings.introduction: A request owns more than the act of starting goroutines. It must know when its work has stopped and who retains the results. Go 1.25 added WaitGroup.Go, which combines task registration and launch. It reduces a common Add/launch ordering mistake without supplying cancellation, an error result or a concurrency budget.
readings.nuance: Use an error-aware group for returned task errors and keep a separate bounded cancellation path for work that may block.
readings.objective: Use modern WaitGroup task ownership and explain its limits.
readings.question: Which capabilities do WaitGroup.Go and Wait provide for owned goroutines?
readings.reviewAnswer: Task registration and a join

sections.body: Each task writes to a distinct fixed result slot, and the owner reads results after Wait. That separates mutation by index without concurrently appending to a shared slice. Do not copy an already used WaitGroup or start an unrelated task after the owner has concluded that the group is empty.
sections.title: Register and join owned work
sections.walkthrough: This complete Go 1.25+ example relies on modern loop-declared variables, distinct output elements and an explicit join. It launches only three tasks. A production version with many inputs still needs admission control before launch, and result values must not share unsafe internal storage.

sections.body: The task function passed to WaitGroup.Go must not panic. It has no error return. Expected failures need an explicit result channel or an error-aware task group, and panic handling belongs to a deliberately chosen boundary. A WaitGroup cannot roll back side effects from a task that already ran.
sections.title: Do not infer an error protocol

sections.body: Wait does not take a context or kill a blocked task. A task doing I/O or sending a result must observe cancellation at each potentially blocking point. On shutdown, stop intake, signal cancellation where appropriate, wait for owned tasks and only then close the resources they use.
sections.title: Give cancellation its own path

sections.body: Use synchronization or a virtual-time test to hold a task at a known boundary. Verify the owner does not publish success until all required work finishes. A sleep followed by checking a counter depends on timing and may hide the same bug on a slower machine.
sections.title: Test completion rather than scheduling luck

readings.takeaway: WaitGroup.Go registers owned work and Wait joins it. Cancellation, errors, panic policy and admission control remain separate parts of the design.
readings.title: WaitGroup.Go joins tasks; it does not collect their errors
wrongAnswers: Cancel the blocked send automatically
Collect and return its error

cautions: Use the bubble for a deterministic in-process protocol and retain isolated integration tests for external services.
designGuide.cost: Choose the policy from the actual contract, then verify its failure path in the target environment.
designGuide.family: Test time and cancellation without sleeping on the wall clock
strengths: Use testing/synctest to assert a concurrent timeline deterministically.
Describe the timeline and assert both early and final states. Virtual time makes supported concurrent tests reproducible; it does not replace real boundary integration checks.

readings.hint: Separate in-process evidence from an external system boundary.
readings.introduction: Tests that sleep for a guessed interval are slow and sensitive to machine load. testing/synctest is a standard package in Go 1.25 and later. It runs a test bubble with virtual time and coordinated goroutine waiting. It is useful for in-process protocols, not a simulator for a remote database or every operating-system event.
readings.nuance: Use the bubble for a deterministic in-process protocol and retain isolated integration tests for external services.
readings.objective: Use testing/synctest to assert a concurrent timeline deterministically.
readings.question: What does a supported testing/synctest bubble control, rather than real remote-service behavior?
readings.reviewAnswer: Time inside a supported test bubble

sections.body: Suppose work waits five seconds, publishes a result and exits. The test should establish that it has not published before the deadline and has completed after it. synctest.Wait lets in-bubble goroutines settle at supported blocking points so the assertions do not depend on the scheduler getting lucky.
sections.title: State the timeline first
sections.walkthrough: Save this complete example as timeline_test.go in a native Go 1.25+ module and run go test -race. The five-second sleep advances virtual time instead of imposing five seconds of wall-clock waiting. This lesson is a reading; it does not promise this diagnostic package on every WASI target.

sections.body: Model a worker waiting on either its timer or ctx.Done, then cancel at a known phase. Assert that the worker closes its completion signal and does not publish an unwanted result. Cancellation and a simultaneously ready result still need a documented policy; select is not a strict priority rule.
sections.title: Add a cancellation branch

sections.body: Virtual time advances when the package can establish the relevant in-bubble blocking state. External network servers, syscalls and objects outside the bubble have different constraints. Keep real integration tests for sockets and databases rather than treating a fast virtual-time test as evidence of remote behavior.
sections.title: Know the boundary of the bubble

sections.body: A deterministic test must still assert something meaningful. For a retry protocol, count durable effects and total attempts under a deadline; for cancellation, prove exit with a completion signal. A test that merely waits for the bubble to finish does not verify every business result.
sections.title: Keep the invariant after removing sleeps

readings.takeaway: Describe the timeline and assert both early and final states. Virtual time makes supported concurrent tests reproducible; it does not replace real boundary integration checks.
readings.title: Test time and cancellation without sleeping on the wall clock
wrongAnswers: That real network failover was tested
That every goroutine schedule is safe

cautions: SetLimit bounds active group functions, not every queued byte. All started work must be joined before its dependencies are released.
designGuide.cost: Choose the policy from the actual contract, then verify its failure path in the target environment.
designGuide.family: errgroup: errors, cancellation and a real concurrency limit
strengths: Coordinate fallible parallel work without confusing cancellation with joining.
Choose one owner for submission, cancellation, joining and result publication. An error-aware group simplifies coordination but does not supply a durable transaction or every admission policy.

readings.hint: The derived context belongs to the group operation.
readings.introduction: golang.org/x/sync/errgroup is a versioned external module, not part of sync. WithContext supplies a derived cancellation context and Wait returns a task error. Tasks must still cooperate with cancellation, and a limit on active tasks is different from a limit on queued input bytes or waiting requests.
readings.nuance: SetLimit bounds active group functions, not every queued byte. All started work must be joined before its dependencies are released.
readings.objective: Coordinate fallible parallel work without confusing cancellation with joining.
readings.question: Which fact must guide reuse of an errgroup-derived context after Wait returns successfully?
readings.reviewAnswer: Wait ends the derived context

sections.body: A group cancels its derived context when a task returns a non-nil error or when Wait returns. Keep that context inside the operation. Even a successful Wait leaves it canceled, so later independent work must use the caller’s appropriate context instead.
sections.title: Use the derived context for the owned operation
sections.walkthrough: This native function-body fragment uses the errgroup package, modern loop declarations, a preallocated output slice and a context-aware load function. The simple submission loop assumes load always exits on cancellation. The group does not deep-copy returned values.

sections.body: Go waits for room when the group is at its configured limit; that admission wait is not itself a ctx-select operation. Do not change the limit while tasks are active. TryGo can express nonblocking admission when the caller has a rejection policy. A fixed worker pool may fit a streaming or explicitly bounded queue better.
sections.title: Understand where SetLimit blocks

sections.body: Production submission may fail before every task is added. Do not return and close dependencies while already started tasks still use them. Cancel the operation and call Wait on every exit path that has launched work. Returning from a helper is not a join; a surrounding owner must enforce that lifecycle.
sections.title: Join after a submission failure

sections.body: A failed group may have populated some result slots before cancellation. Decide whether the operation permits partial success and represent it explicitly. For all-or-nothing results, return no successful result after Wait fails. Database transactions and idempotency still decide which external effects survive.
sections.title: Separate partial results from successful results

readings.takeaway: Choose one owner for submission, cancellation, joining and result publication. An error-aware group simplifies coordination but does not supply a durable transaction or every admission policy.
readings.title: errgroup: errors, cancellation and a real concurrency limit
wrongAnswers: Always the now-canceled group context
A new context with no owner or budget

cautions: A larger connection cap can move waiting into an overloaded database. Admission and query efficiency still need their own policies.
designGuide.cost: Choose the policy from the actual contract, then verify its failure path in the target environment.
designGuide.family: SQL: one pool, explicit capacity and observable waiting

Distinguish the availability/consistency tradeoff during a partition from ordinary latency and throughput tradeoffs even when the network is healthy.
sections.title: Work through the example
sections.walkthrough: Three acknowledgements meet a simple majority threshold for five configured replicas; two do not. The predicate demonstrates arithmetic only. Real consensus also needs terms, log ordering, membership changes, persistence and safety rules. Counting arbitrary replies does not prove a linearizable write or that a stale leader cannot act.

sections.body: Do not claim that a system simply chooses any two of consistency, availability and partition tolerance. A timestamp or a mutex in each replica does not establish a global order. A quorum slogan does not replace a protocol or fault test. Demonstrate split connectivity, stale leadership, concurrent writes, membership changes and recovery, then explain the exact guarantee your operation can still make.
sections.title: Production decisions

sections.body: Does a majority-count helper by itself implement linearizable distributed storage? No. A consistency protocol also needs durable ordering, authority and membership rules; define the guarantee and failure policy of each operation. Describe the state before the operation, its owner, the failure between steps and the evidence you would test. Distinguish what this example demonstrates from the infrastructure a production service still needs.
sections.title: Explain it in an interview

readings.takeaway: Choose per-operation consistency and failure behavior instead of treating CAP as a product rating. No. A consistency protocol also needs durable ordering, authority and membership rules; define the guarantee and failure policy of each operation.
readings.title: Consistency under partitions: explain an operation, not a slogan
wrongAnswers: A local mutex orders writes across replicas
Counting replies implements a consensus algorithm

solutions.core.unused-is-an-error:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	host := "localhost"
	port := 8080
	fmt.Println(host, port)
}

lessons.explanation:
Every Go variable starts at its type's zero value: `0` for numbers, `""` for strings, `false` for booleans, and `nil` for pointers, slices, maps, channels, functions and interfaces. A declaration gives you a defined value immediately.

A struct starts with every field at its own zero value. Design that state to be useful when possible: counters and slices work naturally, while a map field still needs initialization before a write. A `New` function is useful when the type requires setup that its zero value cannot provide.
lessons.objective: Predict the value of any declared variable before it is assigned.

predict.answer:
0 "" true 0

The zero value of a slice is nil. Its length and capacity are 0. You can range over it or append to it; append returns the resulting slice. Indexing the empty slice to read or write an element is out of bounds.
predict.question: What does this print, and why does len work on a nil slice?

lessons.title: Nothing is uninitialised

lessons.explanation:
`:=` declares and assigns in one step inside a function. At least one non-blank name on the left must be new in the current block; otherwise the compiler reports "no new variables".

A short declaration may mix new names with names already declared in that same block. Inside a nested block, however, it may introduce a different variable with the same spelling. Use `=` when the intention is to update an existing variable.
lessons.objective: Choose between := and = without guessing, and know when := is illegal.
lessons.title: := declares, = assigns

lessons.explanation: A useful way to read Go is to ask three questions at each assignment: which block owns this name, what type does it have, and is a new variable being created? The spelling of a name alone does not answer any of them.
lessons.objective: Follow values through a short declaration, an assignment and a shadowed name without running the program.
lessons.title: Read a declaration one scope at a time

lessons.explanation: An error result is part of a function contract. The caller needs to know whether a value is valid when err is non-nil, who should add context, and which layer decides what the user sees. A short early return makes that contract visible.
lessons.objective: Trace a result and error through a complete boundary, including wrapping and partial results.
lessons.title: Read the failure path before the happy path

lessons.explanation:
Go functions can return several values. A common fallible signature returns a result followed by `error`; callers inspect that error before continuing with the result.

This makes ordinary failures explicit at the call site instead of using exceptions. Go also has `panic` and `recover` for exceptional control flow, but an error result is the usual contract for an expected failure. Short failure branches keep the successful path easy to read.
lessons.objective: Write a function that returns a result and an error, and read one.
lessons.title: Two returns instead of one exception

lessons.explanation:
Go refuses to compile a function with a variable it never reads, and a file with an import it never uses. Not a warning — an error.

This feels hostile for about a week. What it buys is that dead code cannot accumulate quietly, and that a half-finished edit fails loudly instead of shipping. The escape hatch when you genuinely need it is assignment to _, which says "deliberately discarded" out loud.
lessons.idiomaticSolution:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	host := "localhost"
	port := 8080
	fmt.Println(host, port)
}
lessons.objective: Recognise the two unused errors on sight and know why they exist.
lessons.title: An unused variable stops the build

lessons.explanation:
An untyped constant in Go has arbitrary precision and no type until it is used. `const big = 1 << 62` is fine even where an int is 32 bits, because nothing has asked it to become an int yet. The moment it is assigned or passed, it takes the type it is needed as — and that is where it can fail to fit.

`iota` is the other half. Inside a const block it counts from zero, one step per line, which is how Go writes enumerations without an enum keyword. The idiom is worth recognising on sight: a type, a const block with iota, and often a String method.
lessons.objective: Explain why 1 << 40 compiles as a constant but overflows as an int32.

predict.question: What does this print?
predict.source:
package main

import "fmt"

type Level int

const (
	Debug Level = iota
	Info
	Warn
	Error

func main() {
	fmt.Println(Debug, Info, Warn, Error)
	const big = 1 << 40
	fmt.Println(big / 1024 / 1024 / 1024)
}

lessons.title: Constants have no type until they need one

lessons.explanation:
In C, Java and JavaScript a case runs on into the next one unless you write `break`. Go inverted that: a case ends at the next case, and `fallthrough` is the keyword you write on the rare occasion you want the old behaviour. You do not need `break` just to end a case, though an explicit `break` can leave a switch early.

Two more differences worth having: a case can list several values separated by commas, and a switch with no expression is a tidy way to write a chain of conditions.
lessons.objective: Write a Go switch without reaching for break.
lessons.title: switch does not fall through

lessons.explanation:
There is no implicit numeric conversion in Go. An int and an int64 are different types even where they are the same width, and adding them is an error rather than a promotion. The fix is always an explicit conversion, and the point of the rule is that the place where precision could be lost is visible in the source.

A named type behaves the same way. `type Celsius float64` cannot be added to a float64 without saying so, which is exactly what makes named types worth declaring: the compiler stops you mixing units.
lessons.idiomaticSolution: return sum / Celsius(len(readings))
lessons.objective: Fix a mismatched-type expression without guessing.
lessons.title: Go never converts a number for you

lessons.explanation:
Names in a function's result list declare local result variables initialized to zero. A bare `return` returns their current values. In a short helper, names such as `quot` and `rem` can explain which result is which.

An explicit `return quot, rem` is often easier to review once a function has branches. Result names document intent, but the compiler does not protect two same-typed results from being swapped. A deferred closure may change named results before the function returns to its caller.
lessons.objective: Write a short function that uses a naked return, and know when not to.
lessons.title: A return can name what it is handing back

lessons.explanation:
Deferred calls run in last-in, first-out order when the surrounding function returns. Three `defer fmt.Println(n)` statements execute in the reverse of their registration order.

The deferred function and its arguments are evaluated when `defer` executes. A deferred closure, in contrast, may read a captured variable when it eventually runs. Keep that distinction clear when a variable changes between registration and return.
lessons.objective: Say the print order of three deferred calls.

done
2

0

lessons.title: Deferred calls stack, last one first

units.summary: Declarations, zero values, multiple returns and the shapes Go repeats everywhere.
units.title: Go core
units.translationNote: Most of this unit is not new material — it is unlearning. Go has no built-in class constructors or exception-handling syntax, and declared variables start with zero values, so habits from Java, C# and Python each need one specific adjustment rather than a general rewrite.

lessons.explanation:
A struct groups fields under a type name. `Point{X: 1, Y: 2}` names its fields; `Point{1, 2}` relies on declaration order. Reordering same-typed fields can silently change an unkeyed literal's meaning. Adding a field usually makes an existing unkeyed literal fail to compile. Keyed literals make intent clearer, and vet checks unkeyed literals for structs from other packages.

A struct's zero value is a struct, not nil. Each field begins at its own zero value. Fields beginning with an uppercase letter are exported; visibility is decided per field.
lessons.objective: Declare a struct type and build values of it without positional guessing.
lessons.title: A struct is data, and its fields have names

lessons.explanation:
A method is declared outside the type, with the receiver in parentheses before the name: `func (r Rect) Area() int`. There is no class body, and methods can be attached to any type you declared in this package — including `type Celsius float64`, not only structs.

The receiver is a copy unless it is a pointer. `func (r Rect) Grow()` mutates a copy and the caller sees nothing; `func (r *Rect) Grow()` mutates the original. Go calls either form for you — `r.Grow()` works on an addressable value whichever receiver you chose — so the compiler will not warn you that the mutation went nowhere.

The convention is to pick one kind of receiver for the whole type. A type with some value methods and some pointer methods has a method set that changes depending on whether you hold a value or a pointer, and that is where "it does not satisfy the interface" comes from.
lessons.objective: Put a method on your own type and choose the receiver deliberately.
lessons.title: A method is a function with a receiver

lessons.explanation:
Go passes everything by value. A struct handed to a function is copied, and writing to the copy changes nothing the caller can see. A pointer is how you say "the same one", and `&` and `*` are the whole syntax: `&value` takes an address, `*pointer` reads through one. Field access needs no `*` — `p.X` works on a pointer as well as a value, which is why you rarely see the star in ordinary code.

There is no pointer arithmetic. A Go pointer either points at something or is nil, and that is all it can do — which is why passing one is safe in a way it is not in C.

The reason to use one is mutation. "Pointers are faster" is a guess: for a small struct the copy is often cheaper than the indirection and the extra work the garbage collector inherits. Measure before believing it, and until you have, choose based on whether the callee needs to change what it was given.
lessons.objective: Say when a pointer is required and when it is only noise.

predict.answer:
1, then 9.

byValue was handed a copy of the struct. It set Retries on the copy,
the copy went out of scope, and the caller's value never changed —
the compiler says nothing, because assigning to your own parameter
is perfectly legal.

byPointer was handed the address, so `s.Retries = 9` wrote through
to the original. Note that neither function needed a `*` to reach
the field: Go dereferences for you on field access.
predict.question: What are the two numbers, and why are they different?

lessons.title: A pointer is for changing something, not for speed

lessons.explanation:
Functions are values: they can be stored, passed and returned. A function literal keeps access to the variables it captures, rather than taking an automatic snapshot of their values.

Two closures capturing the same variable see each other's updates. Separate calls to a factory create separate environments. When you need a snapshot, make an explicit copy for the closure to capture.

Since Go 1.22, iteration variables declared by a loop get a fresh variable on each iteration. A loop assigning to a variable declared outside it still reuses that variable. The distinction between `:=` and `=` matters here too.
lessons.objective: Return a function that carries state, and know what it captured.
lessons.title: A function is a value, and it remembers where it came from

lessons.explanation:
In C this is the classic mistake: return the address of a local and the stack frame is gone by the time the caller looks. Go removes the mistake rather than warning about it. The compiler works out that the value outlives the function — escape analysis — and allocates it somewhere that survives.

So `return &Config{}` is ordinary, idiomatic Go, and constructors called `New...` do it constantly. You are not choosing stack or heap; the compiler is, from how the value is used.

What this does *not* mean is that pointers are free. An escaping value becomes garbage collector work, which is the real cost behind "pointers are faster" being a guess rather than a rule.
lessons.objective: Explain why Go lets you return the address of a local variable.

predict.answer:
It compiles, and prints: a b false

`local` escapes, so the compiler allocates it where it can outlive
the call. Every call to New produces a distinct value, so the two
pointers are different and `first == second` is false — pointer
comparison asks whether they point at the same thing, not whether
the things are equal.
predict.question: Does this compile, and what does it print?

lessons.title: Returning a pointer to a local is fine

units.summary: Structs, methods, pointers, and functions that are values.
units.title: Types you define
units.translationNote:
There is no class here and nothing to inherit from. A struct is data, a method is a function with a receiver written before its name, and the two are declared separately — which means you can put methods on any type you define, not only on structs.

The habit to unlearn is reaching for a pointer by default. In Go a value is copied unless you say otherwise, and that is usually what you want; a pointer is for when the method has to change the thing it was called on, or when copying it would genuinely cost.

lessons.explanation: A slice describes a region of an array. Copying a slice value copies its descriptor, not all the elements. Two descriptors may therefore refer to the same elements while having different lengths and capacities.
lessons.objective: Predict a subslice, an element write and append by tracking the backing array.
lessons.title: A slice is a window, not a copied array

lessons.explanation:
A slice is three words: a pointer to an array, a length and a capacity. append writes into the existing array while the capacity allows it, and allocates a new one when it does not.

That single rule explains most slice surprises: whether a write is seen by another slice depends on whether an append happened to reallocate.
lessons.objective: Predict when append allocates and when it writes in place.

predict.answer:
2 4, then 5 8.

The first append fits in the capacity that was already reserved. The second exceeds it, so the runtime allocates a larger array — the growth factor is an implementation detail, but the doubling to 8 is what current Go does for small slices.
predict.question: What are the two length and capacity pairs?
predict.source:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	s := make([]int, 0, 4)
	s = append(s, 1, 2)
	fmt.Println(len(s), cap(s))
	s = append(s, 3, 4, 5)
	fmt.Println(len(s), cap(s))
}

lessons.title: len is what you have, cap is what you can grow into

lessons.explanation:
Slicing does not copy elements. `s[1:3]` refers to the same backing array, so writes to overlapping elements are visible through both slices. An append that allocates a new array detaches the returned slice from that old storage.

A full slice expression such as `s[1:3:3]` limits capacity, forcing an append of another element to allocate. It does not detach the elements already in the view. Use `copy` or `slices.Clone` when the result must be independently mutable.
lessons.objective: Spot the moment a subslice starts sharing writes with its parent.
lessons.title: Two slices, one array

lessons.explanation: A goroutine does not make its arguments private. If two workers share a slice, you must reason about the slice descriptor and the array it refers to. Making extra goroutines can expose an ownership mistake that a sequential example concealed.
lessons.objective: Separate shared headers, shared elements and safe collection of concurrent results.
lessons.title: Shared slices and concurrent append

lessons.explanation:
Reading a key that is absent returns the value type's zero value, with no error. That is why comma-ok exists: v, ok := m[k] distinguishes "absent" from "present and zero".

The asymmetry to remember: reading from a nil map is legal and returns zero values, but writing to one panics. A map must be made before it can be written.
lessons.objective: Use comma-ok, and know which map operation panics.
lessons.title: Reading a missing key is fine, writing to a nil map is not

lessons.explanation:
A Go string is an immutable sequence of bytes, commonly containing UTF-8. `s[i]` returns one byte and `len(s)` counts bytes.

Ranging over a string decodes UTF-8 and yields each rune with its byte offset. A rune is a Unicode code point, not necessarily a whole displayed character: combining marks and emoji sequences can contain several code points.
lessons.objective: Index, slice and iterate a string without corrupting characters.

predict.answer:
6 5, then 0:h 1:é.

é is two bytes in UTF-8, so the byte length is one more than the rune count, and the offset after é jumps from 1 to 3.
predict.question: Why do the two lengths differ, and which byte offsets appear?

lessons.title: A string is bytes; range gives you runes

lessons.explanation:
Since Go 1.23, `range` accepts a function as well as a slice, map or channel. A function of the shape `func(yield func(V) bool)` is an iterator: it calls `yield` once per element, and stops early when `yield` returns false — which is how a `break` in the caller's loop reaches you.

The language accepts functions that yield zero, one or two values. The standard library names the two value-producing shapes in `iter`: `iter.Seq[V]` yields one value per step, and `iter.Seq2[K, V]` yields two, which is what map-like iteration needs. The zero-value shape is `func(yield func() bool)` and is used with `for range sequence`. These are three language signatures, not three named types in `iter`.

After `yield` returns false, return without calling it again. Do not save yield for later or invoke it from another goroutine. A sequence may own resources, so its early-exit path must release them as well.

The point is not novelty. Before this, a function returning a sequence had to hand back a whole slice — allocating every element even when the caller wanted the first one — or take a callback and lose `break`, `continue` and `return`. An iterator is lazy and keeps the loop keywords working, which is why `slices.Values` and `maps.Keys` return one instead of a copy.
lessons.objective: Write something that can be ranged over without building a slice first.
lessons.title: range works on functions too

lessons.explanation:
A slice has both a length and a capacity, and they gate different things. Indexing is checked against len: `s[i]` panics the moment i reaches len, however much capacity remains behind it. Reslicing is checked against cap: `s[:n]` is legal for any n up to cap, and that is how a slice grows back into space it had already allocated.

This is why `make([]int, 0, 10)` is not indexable at all and `make([]int, 10)` is: the first has room for ten and holds none.
lessons.objective: Say which of two similar-looking index expressions panics.

predict.answer:
3 8
6 8
panic on index
predict.question: What does this print?

lessons.title: len is what you may read; cap is what you may reslice

lessons.explanation: Visible length is not retained memory size. A small view can keep an entire allocation reachable. This is often noticed when a parser, cache or queue stores a few bytes from each large input and memory grows far beyond the stored lengths.
lessons.objective: Recognize retained backing arrays and detach small long-lived results deliberately.
lessons.title: A tiny slice can keep a large buffer alive

lessons.explanation:
The language does not specify map iteration order, and the order may change from one iteration to the next. A small example that repeatedly uses one order does not establish a guarantee.

When output must be deterministic, collect the keys, sort them and read values in that sorted order. When order is irrelevant, test the entries without requiring a particular traversal sequence.
lessons.objective: Produce stable output from a map without hoping.
lessons.title: Map iteration order is not specified

lessons.explanation:
Strings are immutable. Repeated `s += piece` operations in a growing loop can copy the accumulated prefix repeatedly, producing quadratic work as the output grows. Small fixed concatenations may be optimized differently, so measure the actual workload.

`strings.Builder` accumulates text in a growing buffer and exposes the result with `String`. `strings.Join` is a simpler choice when all pieces are already collected. A non-zero Builder must not be copied.
lessons.objective: Use strings.Builder for repeated construction without rebuilding the prefix.
lessons.title: Concatenating in a loop repeatedly rebuilds a string

lessons.explanation:
The Tour's "Creating a slice with make" page and Effective Go's "Allocation with new" page are the same distinction. `new(T)` allocates a zero T and returns `*T`. Since Go 1.26, `new(expr)` can instead initialize the new variable with an expression: `new(42)` returns `*int` pointing at 42. This does not initialize a nil map when the operand is the map type. `make` is only for slices, maps and channels: it returns an initialized value, not a pointer to one.

`new(map[string]int)` is a pointer to a nil map. Writing through it panics. `make(map[string]int)` is a map you can write. The same trap exists for a slice: `new([]int)` is `*[]int` pointing at nil; `make([]int, 0, 8)` is a slice with room. `new(make(map[string]int))` is a pointer to an initialized map, but prefer the map value itself unless pointer-to-map semantics are specifically needed. Older language versions reject the expression form of `new`.
lessons.idiomaticSolution:
func ReadyMap() map[string]int { return make(map[string]int) }
func ZeroCounter() *int        { return new(int) }
lessons.objective: Pick make or new for a slice, a map and a pointer.
lessons.title: make initializes collections; new returns a pointer

lessons.explanation:
The Tour's "Arrays" page is the one people skip because slices are what you use. Then a function signature says `[32]byte` and the compiler refuses a `[16]byte`. The length is in the type: `[4]int` and `[3]int` are as different as `int` and `string`.

An array is a value. Assigning it copies every element. A slice is a header pointing at an array, which is why two slices can share memory and two arrays never do unless you pass a pointer. The conversion is one way and explicit: `s := a[:]` views the array; there is no implicit `[n]T` from a slice of the wrong length.
lessons.objective: Write a function that takes [4]int and returns [3]int.
lessons.title: The length is part of an array's type

lessons.explanation:
The Tour's "Mutating Maps" page is the two-value read: `elem, ok := m[key]`. A missing key and a present zero look the same if you only take `elem`. Scores, counts, flags — anything whose zero is a legitimate stored value — need the ok.

`delete(m, key)` is the other half of that page. Deleting a missing key is a no-op, not an error. After delete, ok is false even if the old value was zero.
lessons.objective: Report whether a key is present when its value can be zero.
lessons.title: Comma-ok is how you tell zero from missing

lessons.explanation:
The Tour's "Nil slices" page: the zero value of a slice is nil, it has length and capacity 0, and it has no backing array. `append` treats that as a valid empty slice and allocates. JSON encodes a nil slice as `null` and a non-nil empty one as `[]` — the only common place the distinction leaks out.

`s == nil` is true for `var s []int` and false for `s := []int{}`. Both have len 0. Prefer `len(s) == 0` unless you are talking to a wire format that cares.
lessons.objective: Predict what len, == nil and append do to a zero slice.

predict.answer:
true 0 0
false 1 1
false 0
predict.question: What does this print?

lessons.title: A nil slice is empty, and append still works

lessons.explanation:
The Tour's "Function values" page: functions are values. They can be arguments and results. The type includes the parameters and the result, so `func(int) int` and `func(int) string` are as different as int and string.

This is not a method and not a generic yet. It is the shape map and filter had in Go before type parameters, and it is still how most callbacks are written.
lessons.objective: Apply a func(int) int to every element of a slice.
lessons.title: A function is a value you can pass

units.summary: Length against capacity, shared backing arrays, and why a string is not a []char.
units.title: Slices, maps and strings
units.translationNote: This is where habits from Python and JavaScript do real damage. A Go slice is a view over an array, not a list object, so two slices can share memory and a third can silently observe your writes.

lessons.explanation:
A type satisfies an interface by having the methods. There is no implements keyword and no import relationship, so a package can accept types that were written before its interface existed.

The idiom that follows: accept interfaces, return structs. And keep the interface as small as the function actually uses — one method is common and two is already a design decision.
lessons.objective: Write the smallest interface a function needs, at the call site.
lessons.title: The consumer declares the interface

lessons.explanation:
A method with a value receiver belongs to both T and *T. A method with a pointer receiver belongs only to *T.

So if any method that satisfies an interface has a pointer receiver, a plain value does not satisfy it — and the compiler says "does not implement", often pointing at a line that looks obviously correct. The fix is nearly always &value rather than changing the receiver.
lessons.objective: Predict whether a value or only a pointer satisfies an interface.

predict.answer:
1.

Add has a pointer receiver, so it is in the method set of *Counter only. `var a adder = c` would not compile.
predict.question: Why must the assignment use &c, and what does this print?

lessons.title: Pointer receiver, pointer method set

lessons.explanation:
An interface value holds a dynamic type and a dynamic value. It is nil only when it holds neither. Assigning a nil `*MyError` to an `error` variable preserves the pointer type, so `err != nil` is true even though its contained pointer is nil.

When a function returns an error interface, return literal `nil` on the success path rather than a typed nil pointer. Calling a method on an interface holding a nil pointer is safe only if that method deliberately supports a nil receiver.
lessons.objective: Explain why err != nil can be true when the error is nil.

predict.answer:
false.

check returns an error interface holding type *PathError with a nil value, and an interface is nil only when its type is nil too. Returning nil explicitly on the success path fixes it.
predict.question: Does this print true or false, and why?

lessons.title: A nil pointer in an interface is not a nil interface

lessons.explanation:
A type assertion has two forms and the difference matters. `v := x.(int)` panics when x is not an int. `v, ok := x.(int)` never panics: ok says whether it worked, and v is the zero value when it did not. In anything that handles input you did not write, the two-value form is the only one.

A type switch is the same question asked about several types at once, and it is how Go writes what other languages do with pattern matching or a visitor.
lessons.objective: Read a value out of an interface without risking a panic.
lessons.title: Asking an interface what it is holding

lessons.explanation:
Writing a type inside a struct without a field name embeds it, and its methods are promoted to the outer type. It looks like inheritance and is not: there is no virtual dispatch and no super. The outer type gets a field it can reach through, and the promoted methods still run against that inner value.

The consequence people trip on: a method the outer type declares shadows the promoted one for outside callers, but a promoted method calling a sibling still calls the inner one. Go resolves this at compile time by name, not at run time by receiver.
lessons.objective: Predict which method runs when an embedded type has one too.

predict.answer:
LOUD ada
hello from base ada
predict.question: What does this print? Look carefully at the second line.

lessons.title: Embedding is not inheritance

lessons.explanation:
`fmt.Stringer` is a small formatting contract:

```go
type Stringer interface { String() string }
```

Common string formatting operations in `fmt` call `String()` when the value implements it. Format verbs that explicitly request another representation may behave differently. No registration is needed.

Do not format the same value through its own String method in a way that calls String again. Convert it to its underlying type or format its fields to avoid recursion.
lessons.objective: Make a type print itself as a dotted IPv4 address.
lessons.title: fmt looks for String(), not a Stringer keyword

lessons.explanation:
The Tour's "The empty interface" page: `interface{}` specifies zero methods, so every type implements it. `any` is the alias. `fmt.Print` takes `...any` for that reason.

Holding a value in `any` throws the static type away. Getting it back is a type assertion or a type switch — the two-value form, or you panic. `%T` in fmt is the cheap way to see what is inside, and it is what this lesson asks you to return.
lessons.objective: Report the dynamic type of a value held in any.
lessons.title: any is interface{}, and it has no methods

units.summary: Implicit satisfaction, method sets, and the nil that is not nil.
units.title: Interfaces
units.translationNote: Nothing declares that it implements an interface. That inverts where abstraction lives: the consumer defines the interface it needs, so the useful interfaces are small and defined next to the code using them, not next to the type satisfying them.

lessons.explanation:
Type parameters go in square brackets before the ordinary ones: `func Map[T, U any](in []T, f func(T) U) []U`. `T` and `U` are types the caller supplies, and in almost every call the compiler infers them so you write `Map(names, length)` with no brackets at all.

`any` is the constraint that allows every type. It is a real alias for `interface{}`, but in this position it means something different: with `interface{}` as a *parameter* type you get a value you must assert your way out of, and with `any` as a *constraint* you get the caller's actual type, checked at compile time.

That is the whole gain. The old version of this function returned `[]interface{}` and every caller unpacked it; the generic one returns `[]U`, and a mistake is a compile error rather than a panic.
lessons.objective: Write a function that works for several types without interface{} and without a cast.
lessons.title: A type parameter is written in square brackets

lessons.explanation:
A constraint says what the compiler may assume about `T`. It is written as an interface — the same keyword — but an interface used as a constraint can list *types* as well as methods:

```
type Number interface {
	~int | ~int64 | ~float64
}
```

The `|` is a union, and the `~` means "any type whose underlying type is this", so `type Celsius float64` satisfies `~float64`. Without the tilde your own named types are excluded, which is almost never what you meant.

The standard library provides `cmp.Ordered` for types that support ordering. `constraints` is not a standard-library package. Reaching for `cmp.Ordered` before writing your own is useful, because a constraint is part of your API and a homemade one is a second vocabulary for readers to learn.
lessons.objective: Constrain a type parameter to what your code actually needs.
lessons.title: A constraint is an interface with types in it

lessons.explanation:
Types take parameters with the same syntax: `type Stack[T any] struct { items []T }`. Methods on it repeat the parameter in the receiver — `func (s *Stack[T]) Push(v T)` — which makes the type's parameter available to the method.

For most of generics' life a method could not introduce a parameter of its own, so transformations to another type were written as functions before Go 1.27. That restriction is gone; the next lesson is about what replaced it.

The zero value still has to work. `var s Stack[int]` gives you a struct whose slice is nil, and appending to a nil slice is fine, so the stack is usable without a constructor — worth designing for rather than stumbling into.

Popping must also clear the obsolete array slot before shortening the slice. Otherwise a stack of pointers, slices or interfaces can keep removed objects reachable while its backing array stays alive. The returned value remains valid; clearing the slot releases only the container's extra reference.

Instantiation is explicit where inference has nothing to work from: `Stack[int]{}` names the type, while `Push(1)` infers nothing because `T` is already fixed by the receiver.
lessons.objective: Write a container that holds one type rather than any type.
lessons.title: A type can take parameters too

lessons.explanation:
Go 1.27 lets a method declare type parameters of its own, in addition to the ones its receiver already carries:

```
type List[E any] []E

func (l List[E]) Apply[F any](f func(E) F) List[F] {
	...
}
```

`E` comes from the receiver; `F` belongs to the method. Before this, the second one had no place to live, so this transformation was commonly written as a package-level function taking the collection as its first argument. That was not a style choice — the language had no way to write it as a method.

Like a generic function, a generic method is instantiated before it is called, and in ordinary code the compiler infers the type argument from what you pass. The judgement from the previous lessons still applies: this removes a restriction, it does not create an obligation. A method earns a type parameter when the transformation genuinely produces a different element type, and not because it now can have one.
lessons.objective: Write the method that could only be a function before Go 1.27.
lessons.title: A method can take its own type parameter

lessons.explanation:
The Go team's own guidance is narrow. Type parameters are for: functions over slices, maps and channels of any element type; general data structures like trees and stacks; and methods that are identical for several types apart from the type itself.

The case against everything else is readability. A generic function has to be read twice — once for what it does and once for what its constraint permits — and it cannot use anything the constraint does not promise, which usually makes it *less* capable than the concrete version it replaced.

Two smells worth naming. If the constraint ends up being an interface with methods and nothing else, an ordinary interface parameter is simpler and does the same thing at the cost of one dynamic dispatch. And if a function has a type parameter used exactly once, in one argument, it is a plain function wearing a costume.
lessons.objective: Recognise the three cases where a type parameter earns its place, and the ones where it does not.

predict.answer:
Both print id-7. Write PrintPlain.

The constraint here is an interface with a method and nothing else,
so the type parameter buys nothing: there is no second type
involved, no container to keep typed, and no operator that needs a
concrete type. What it costs is a signature that has to be read
twice.

The runtime and compiler may handle dispatch and allocation differently.
Neither version guarantees a heap allocation or a performance
advantage; measure before trading clarity for speculation.
predict.question: Both compile and print the same thing. Which should you write, and why?

lessons.title: Most code that could be generic should not be

units.summary: Type parameters, constraints, and the times an interface is the better answer.
units.title: Generics, and when not to
units.translationNote:
If you are coming from Java or C#, the shape will look familiar and the culture will not. Go got type parameters late and on purpose, and the community's default is still to reach for them last — a function that works on one concrete type is not a failure waiting to be generalised.

There is no reflection-based erasure story to learn and no covariance rules to fight. Interfaces describe both ordinary values and type-parameter constraints. A constraint with type terms is not an ordinary value type: use it to bound a type parameter.

lessons.explanation:
fmt.Errorf with %w produces an error that both reads well and still contains the original. errors.Is and errors.As walk that chain.

Two conventions make the chain readable: error strings are lowercase and unpunctuated because they get concatenated, and each layer adds only what it uniquely knows — usually the operation and its input.
lessons.objective: Wrap an error so callers can still match the original.
lessons.title: %w adds context without hiding the cause

lessons.explanation:
errors.Is asks whether anything in the chain equals a sentinel. errors.As asks whether anything in the chain is a particular type, and gives it to you so you can read its fields.

Sentinel when the caller only needs to know which kind of failure it was; typed error when the caller needs a detail, such as which field was invalid.
lessons.objective: Choose between errors.Is and errors.As without trial and error.
lessons.title: Is compares, As extracts

lessons.explanation:
A deferred call runs when the function returns, whichever return it was, and deferred calls run in reverse order. That is what makes acquire-then-defer-release safe against every early return an error check introduces.

The argument to a deferred call is evaluated immediately; only the call is postponed. This surprises people exactly once.
lessons.objective: Release what you acquired, in the right order, on every path.

predict.answer:
end 3 2 1

Each defer captured its own i by value at the moment it was deferred, and the deferred calls run in reverse order.
predict.question: In what order do the numbers print?

lessons.title: defer runs last in, first out

lessons.explanation:
`error` is an interface with one method, so anything with `Error() string` is one. That is what makes an error able to carry structured information: a field for the line that failed, the value that was rejected, the operation that was attempted.

`errors.As` is the counterpart to `errors.Is`. Where Is asks "is this that particular error", As asks "is there an error of this type anywhere in the chain, and if so give it to me" — which is how a caller reads those fields back out after the error has been wrapped.
lessons.objective: Write an error that carries data the caller can read.
lessons.title: An error is any type with an Error method

lessons.explanation:
A file that will not open is a failure: it is expected, the caller can do something about it, and it is an error value. An index past the end of a slice is a bug: the program's own logic is wrong, and continuing would be worse than stopping. Go draws that line deliberately, and a library that panics on bad input has drawn it in the wrong place.

`recover` exists, and its honest use is narrow: stopping one request from taking down a server, at the boundary, before returning an ordinary error. It is not a catch block, and using it as one hides the bug that caused it.
lessons.objective: Say which of two situations deserves a panic.

predict.answer:
fine
<nil>
recovered: bad state
predict.question: What does this print? Note that err is a named return.

lessons.title: panic is for bugs, not for failures

lessons.explanation:
The Tour shows panic as a value and Effective Go keeps recover for a server boundary: one request, one goroutine, then an ordinary error back to the caller. `recover` only works inside a deferred function. A named result is how that error gets out — a `return nil` after `work()` would overwrite it.

A library that recovers in the middle of a calculation is hiding a bug. A process that recovers at main is pretending the program is still sound. The honest width is one unit of work you can abandon.
lessons.objective: Turn a panic into an error without swallowing the rest of the program.
lessons.title: recover belongs at the boundary

units.summary: Wrapping, errors.Is and errors.As, sentinels, defer and the panic boundary.
units.title: Errors
units.translationNote: There is no catch. An error is a value you return, and the caller decides. What replaces a stack trace is a chain of wrapped context, built deliberately at each level that knows something the level below did not.

lessons.explanation:
`go.mod` names the module, such as `example.com/forge`. A package in `internal/build` is then imported using `example.com/forge/internal/build`.

The import path locates the package; its `package` clause determines the default name used in source. The name often matches the last directory component, but does not have to. An import alias can choose another local name.

An `internal` directory also enforces an import boundary: only code within the tree rooted at its parent may import that package.
lessons.objective: Predict the import path of any package in a module.

predict.answer:
import "example.com/forge/internal/build"

The importer must have an import path within the example.com/forge tree. A separate module named example.com/forge/client can satisfy that rule; other.example/client cannot. The boundary follows the parent import-path tree, rather than the identity of the module.
predict.question: How does cmd/forge/main.go import Run, and could a different module do the same?

lessons.title: The import path is the module path plus the directory

lessons.explanation:
An identifier starting with an upper-case letter is visible outside its package; anything else is not. There is no public, private or protected.

Because the name carries the visibility, renaming is an API change, and Go's naming conventions get unusually strict: no stuttering (build.Runner, not build.BuildRunner), no Get prefix on getters, and short names for short-lived variables.
lessons.objective: Control visibility without keywords, and name things accordingly.
lessons.title: A capital letter is the access modifier

lessons.explanation:
A test is a function such as `func TestParse(t *testing.T)` in a file ending `_test.go`. It can use the production package name, or a package name ending `_test` to exercise the exported API from outside the package.

A table-driven test keeps cases in data and the assertion in code. `t.Run` gives each case a separate name in the result stream. No external test framework is required.
lessons.objective: Write a table-driven test and run it locally.
lessons.title: Tests are a file, not a framework

lessons.explanation:
A package's name becomes the qualifier callers read: `http.Server` is clearer than `http.HTTPServer`. Prefer short, descriptive lowercase names. Singular names are common, but useful standard-library packages such as `strings`, `errors` and `slices` are plural.

Avoid needless repetition between package and exported name. `chart.New` can be clear for a package centered on one chart type; a package with several constructors may need more specific names. Read the whole selector to judge it.
lessons.objective: Name a package and its exported function without repeating yourself.

predict.answer:
GO
true
b3w4r3
predict.question: What does this print?

lessons.title: The package name is half the API

lessons.explanation:
A package initializes its variables using their dependency relationships, then runs its init functions in source order as presented to the compiler. Imported packages finish initialization before the importing package. `main` starts after the program's initialization completes.

Do not depend on arbitrary file presentation order for important behavior. Explicit constructors make configuration and recoverable failure handling visible. An init function takes no arguments and returns no result, though it can register a driver or format as a deliberate import side effect.
lessons.objective: Predict the order of package variables, init and main.

predict.answer:
var first
var second
init
main first second
predict.question: In what order do the lines appear?

lessons.title: init runs before main, and order is defined

lessons.explanation: A repository, a module and a package can be three different boundaries. Trace the module path plus the package subdirectory before changing imports. A version suffix is part of the import identity; a folder name alone does not decide which source the compiler builds.
lessons.objective: Resolve module roots, import paths, internal visibility and major-version suffixes.
lessons.title: A module is a release boundary; a package is a directory

lessons.explanation: A direct require is not a lock on every transitive dependency. Other requirements can raise the selected version of the same module path. Diagnose the graph first, then test the change that actually enters the build; repeatedly deleting go.sum does not explain an upgrade.
lessons.objective: Read minimal version selection and investigate a transitive upgrade without guessing.
lessons.title: Explain the selected version before running go get

lessons.explanation: A download failure may come from version discovery, credentials, a proxy, the checksum database or local cache integrity. Treat those as separate layers. A checksum records content identity; it neither proves the code is safe nor decides which version the dependency graph chooses.
lessons.objective: Diagnose downloads without leaking private paths or disabling integrity checks globally.
lessons.title: Checksums, proxies and private modules solve different problems

lessons.explanation: A checkout can pass because go.work supplies a sibling module or replace points to a local directory that no consumer has. That success tests the local composition, not the published module. Keep a second path that exercises the version and files a real downstream user receives.
lessons.objective: Use go.work and replace for development while checking what an independent consumer builds.
lessons.title: A local workspace can hide a broken release

lessons.explanation: A successful build in your checkout can depend on uncommitted generated files, platform-specific source or an asset missing from the release archive. Reproducibility concerns the whole input set: toolchain, selected modules, build constraints, generated files and embedded data.
lessons.objective: Check the source and assets that a clean build actually receives.
lessons.title: Reproduce the artifact: vendor, build tags and embedded files

lessons.explanation: A test can pass alone and fail when other packages or subtests run at the same time. Shared database names, environment variables, ports and mutable globals turn isolated test intent into interference. Give every test its own resources, and distinguish a data race from a wider coordination bug.
lessons.objective: Find races, test caching mistakes and shared integration fixtures before scaling concurrency.
lessons.title: Parallel tests must own their mutable resources

lessons.explanation: An ns/op number describes one workload in one process. A production incident may instead come from pool wait, queue growth, a slow downstream service or allocation pressure. Start with the question you need to answer and preserve the workload and environment alongside the measurement.
lessons.objective: Measure allocations, concurrency and tail latency without mistaking closed-loop throughput for service capacity.
lessons.title: A microbenchmark is not a capacity test

lessons.explanation: A high-latency request does not necessarily consume much CPU. It may be waiting on a mutex, scheduling, a network response or a connection pool. Capture evidence for the same workload and time window, and choose a profile that can explain the suspected delay.
lessons.objective: Use pprof and traces to investigate latency under load instead of increasing pools blindly.
lessons.title: Profile CPU, allocation and waiting as different bottlenecks

lessons.explanation: A burst of parallel compilation can exhaust memory before the program you are testing even starts. Build-cache misses, many packages, cgo and simultaneous jobs change the working set. Read the exact failing phase instead of assuming every slowdown is a goroutine scheduling issue in application code.
lessons.objective: Separate compiler work, runtime goroutines and caches when CI or a small machine stalls.
lessons.title: Build concurrency also has a memory budget

lessons.explanation: The binary that formats, generates or analyzes your project is part of the workflow’s input. An unpinned command on PATH can silently change generated output or lint results. Keep the intended tool version and compiler selection explicit without confusing them with the libraries your application imports.
lessons.objective: Distinguish application dependencies, development commands and toolchain selection.
lessons.title: Pin the compiler and the tools that generate your code

lessons.explanation: Normal tests often cover the examples you already understand. Parsers and protocol boundaries also receive truncated, oversized and surprising inputs. Fuzzing explores input behavior, while vulnerability analysis asks whether known vulnerable code is reachable; the two tools answer different questions.
lessons.objective: Combine fuzzing, regression seeds and govulncheck without treating one green tool as complete assurance.
lessons.title: Test unknown inputs and check reachable vulnerabilities

lessons.explanation: Imported packages initialize before main, and hidden setup can turn an import into a database connection, network wait or process-wide configuration decision. Make those dependencies visible at the composition root so startup, tests, retries and shutdown share a clear owner.
lessons.objective: Move fallible setup to an explicit owner and close shared resources after work drains.
lessons.title: Package initialization is not a request-time connection factory

units.summary: Import paths, go.mod, go test and go vet, without a search engine.
units.title: Packages, modules and tooling
units.translationNote: Go's survey found professionals repeatedly returning to documentation for core go subcommands. That is not a knowledge gap so much as a model gap: once the module, the import path and the package directory line up in your head, the commands stop needing to be memorised.

lessons.explanation:
A send on an unbuffered channel does not complete until a receiver takes the value, and a receive does not complete until a sender provides one. It is a rendezvous, not a mailbox.

This is why the classic first Go deadlock is one line long: send on an unbuffered channel from the only goroutine there is, and nobody can ever arrive to meet it. The runtime notices that every goroutine is asleep and stops the program, which is a much better failure than a silent hang.
lessons.objective: Say what blocks, and for how long, on a channel with no buffer.

predict.answer:
It deadlocks: fatal error: all goroutines are asleep - deadlock!

The send blocks waiting for a receiver, and the only goroutine that could receive is the one already blocked sending. make(chan string, 1) would let the send complete into the buffer, and the program would print hello.
predict.question: What happens, and would a buffer of one change it?

lessons.title: An unbuffered channel is a meeting

lessons.explanation:
go f() starts f and immediately continues. There is no future to await and no value to collect, so the result has to come back through a channel or a shared variable protected by something.

The second half matters just as much: when main returns, the program exits and every remaining goroutine simply stops. A goroutine still blocked at that moment did not fail — it was never finished.
lessons.objective: Get a result out of a goroutine, and know when the program stops waiting.

predict.answer:
No.

main returns as soon as it receives from results, and nothing makes it wait for the second goroutine. It may print, may not, and the program is wrong either way if the output matters.
predict.question: Is the second goroutine guaranteed to print?
predict.source:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	results := make(chan int)
	go func() { results <- 42 }()
	go func() { fmt.Println("this may never print") }()
	fmt.Println(<-results)
}

lessons.title: go returns nothing

lessons.explanation: Starting a goroutine creates an obligation: identify who asks it to stop and who observes that it has stopped. Canceling a context closes a signal; it does not terminate arbitrary Go code. Every blocking point must cooperate or have another bounded exit.
lessons.objective: Design a worker so it can stop waiting and its owner can wait for it to finish.
lessons.title: Cancellation is a request; joining proves exit

lessons.explanation:
Closing a channel says that no more values will be sent. Give that decision to the producer, or to a coordinator that knows all producers have finished. A receiver should not close a stream while senders may still use it.

Receivers can drain a closed buffered channel. `v, ok := <-ch` reports false only when the channel is closed and empty; `for v := range ch` then ends. Sending after close and closing twice both panic.
lessons.objective: Decide who closes a channel, and why the other side must not.
lessons.title: The sender closes, the receiver ranges

lessons.explanation:
select blocks until one of its cases can proceed, and picks randomly among those that are ready. Adding a case for <-ctx.Done() turns any wait into a cancellable one.

The convention that makes this composable: context is the first parameter, it is passed rather than stored, and cancel is always deferred so the resources behind it are released on every path.
lessons.objective: Make a blocking operation cancellable without a flag or a kill switch.
lessons.title: select waits on several things; context says stop

lessons.explanation:
A channel is useful for transferring values and coordinating ownership. A mutex protects shared state that remains in place. Choose the mechanism that makes the invariant and its owner easiest to understand; neither mechanism is always faster.
