Keep the mutex next to the data it protects and use the same locking rule for every read and write participating in the invariant. A small, clearly bounded critical section is easier to maintain than a lock whose protected state is scattered.
lessons.objective: Choose between a mutex and a channel for a given problem.
lessons.title: A mutex is for state; a channel is for handing over

lessons.explanation:
A fixed number of workers bounds concurrent processing. The producer sends jobs and closes the input stream after the last job. Workers consume it until it is drained. A coordinator waits for every worker before closing the output stream.

Results may need to be consumed while jobs are still being produced, or backpressure can deadlock the producer and workers. Add cancellation deliberately, and test termination as well as returned values.
lessons.objective: Build a fixed set of workers that finishes cleanly.
lessons.title: The worker pool, written once

lessons.explanation: Concurrency is how work overlaps. Capacity is how much useful work the system can sustain. A thousand waiting goroutines do not give Redis a thousand extra cores or increase a database connection budget. They do consume memory, queue time and cancellation bookkeeping.
lessons.objective: Bound active workers and queued work according to the resource that actually limits throughput.
lessons.title: More goroutines are not more capacity

lessons.explanation:
The Tour's "Buffered Channels" page: `make(chan int, 100)` sends without a receiver until the buffer is full, and receives without a sender until it is empty. An unbuffered channel is a rendezvous. A buffered one is a mailbox of a known size.

The deadlock people then write is filling a buffer of 1 with two sends from the only goroutine there is. The buffer does not make the channel unbounded. It makes the bound visible in the `make`.
lessons.objective: Send n values on a channel of capacity n without another goroutine.
lessons.title: A buffer is a mailbox, not a meeting

lessons.explanation:
The Tour's "Range and Close" page: `v, ok := <-ch` sets ok to false once the channel is closed and empty. `for v := range ch` is that loop written once. Only the sender closes. Sending after a close panics. Closing is not required for the garbage collector — only for telling a range there is nothing more.

Channels are not files. Most of them never close, because nobody is ranging. Close when a range (or an ok-receive) needs the signal.
lessons.objective: Drain a channel with range, and close it from the sender.
lessons.title: range over a channel ends when it closes

lessons.explanation:
The Tour's "Default Selection" page: a `default` case runs when no other case is ready, so the select returns instead of blocking. That is how you poll a channel, and how you try a send without parking the goroutine.

Without default, select waits. With it, "nothing ready" is a value you handle, not a hang. A busy loop of default-selects is a spin; use it for a single try, not as a substitute for a timer.
lessons.objective: Receive from a channel if a value is ready, and return if it is not.
lessons.title: default makes select try, not wait

lessons.explanation:
The Tour writes `ch <- v` and `v := <-ch` and then, in Effective Go, the type itself carries the arrow: `chan<- int` is send-only, `<-chan int` is receive-only. A function that only produces values should take `chan<- T`. The compiler then refuses a receive in that body, which is the whole point — the restriction is the API.

Conversion is one way: a bidirectional channel may be passed where a directional one is wanted. The other direction does not compile. Close is a send-side operation, so it belongs on `chan<- T`.
lessons.objective: Write a producer that takes chan<- int and closes it.
lessons.title: The arrow in the type is who may send

lessons.explanation:
Effective Go and the sync docs: `Once.Do(f)` runs f once, even when many goroutines call Do at the same time. After that, Do is a no-op. It is the right shape for a lazy setup that must not run twice — registering a driver, reading a config, seeding a generator.

Do not copy an Once after it has been used. Do not call Do with a different f and expect that second f to run. The once is on the Once, not on the function value.
lessons.objective: Initialise shared state without a lock you have to remember.
lessons.title: sync.Once runs a function one time, for everyone

lessons.explanation: A request owns more than the act of starting goroutines. It must know when its work has stopped and who retains the results. Go 1.25 added WaitGroup.Go, which combines task registration and launch. It reduces a common Add/launch ordering mistake without supplying cancellation, an error result or a concurrency budget.
lessons.objective: Use modern WaitGroup task ownership and explain its limits.
lessons.title: WaitGroup.Go joins tasks; it does not collect their errors

lessons.explanation: Tests that sleep for a guessed interval are slow and sensitive to machine load. testing/synctest is a standard package in Go 1.25 and later. It runs a test bubble with virtual time and coordinated goroutine waiting. It is useful for in-process protocols, not a simulator for a remote database or every operating-system event.
lessons.objective: Use testing/synctest to assert a concurrent timeline deterministically.
lessons.title: Test time and cancellation without sleeping on the wall clock

lessons.explanation: golang.org/x/sync/errgroup is a versioned external module, not part of sync. WithContext supplies a derived cancellation context and Wait returns a task error. Tasks must still cooperate with cancellation, and a limit on active tasks is different from a limit on queued input bytes or waiting requests.
lessons.objective: Coordinate fallible parallel work without confusing cancellation with joining.
lessons.title: errgroup: errors, cancellation and a real concurrency limit

lessons.explanation: An atomic load or store synchronizes an operation on the atomic value. It does not recursively make the object graph immutable or protect a later map mutation. A useful read-mostly pattern builds a complete independent configuration, publishes one pointer and lets readers hold that immutable snapshot. All fields that must agree belong to the same published value.
lessons.objective: Publish one consistent snapshot and preserve ownership of its reachable maps and slices.
lessons.title: Atomic publication is safe only when the published snapshot stays immutable

lessons.explanation: The presence of a mutex in a struct does not prove that every operation locks the same mutex. A value receiver or assignment can copy the lock while retaining a reference to the same map. Likewise, sync.Map protects its own operations but cannot infer an invariant spanning several keys. Define the state that must change together and keep one synchronization owner for that state.
lessons.objective: Choose synchronization around related state and return snapshots rather than copied lock owners.
lessons.title: Mutex, RWMutex and sync.Map: protect the invariant and do not copy the lock

units.summary: Goroutines, channel ownership, select, buffers and who may send.
units.title: Concurrency
units.translationNote: A goroutine is not a promise and not a thread. It has no handle, no return value and no join — which is why channels and WaitGroups exist, and why "who closes this channel" is a design question rather than a detail.

lessons.explanation:
io.Reader has Read. io.Writer has Write. Files, network connections, HTTP bodies, gzip streams, strings.Reader and bytes.Buffer all satisfy one or both.

Accepting them instead of a concrete type is what makes Go code testable without mocks: the test passes a bytes.Buffer and reads the result back.
lessons.objective: Write a function that works on a file, a string and a test buffer.
lessons.title: Two interfaces, one method each

lessons.explanation:
encoding/json maps struct fields by name, and a tag overrides that. Only exported fields are considered, which is the first thing that catches people: a lower-case field is invisible to the encoder with no error.

Unmarshal leaves fields absent from the input untouched rather than zeroing them, so decoding into a reused struct can silently keep old values.
lessons.objective: Control field names, omit empties, and know what unmarshalling leaves untouched.

predict.answer:
{"host":"localhost"}

port was zero and carries omitempty, so it is dropped. secret is unexported, so encoding/json cannot see it at all — no tag would change that.
predict.question: What is printed, and where did port and secret go?

lessons.title: Struct tags are the JSON schema

lessons.explanation: Go 1.27 includes encoding/json/v2 without an experiment flag. Keeping encoding/json preserves its v1 behavior; adopting the v2 API is a separate decision. A compiling change can still alter a mobile model, persisted event or generated client. Write the expected wire representation before migrating.
lessons.objective: Compare null, empty and omitted JSON values before changing a public API.
lessons.title: JSON v2: migrate behavior, not just imports

lessons.explanation:
`time.Duration` is an int64 counting nanoseconds, and the constants are what make it readable: `5 * time.Second` is a multiplication, not a function call. That is also the trap — a bare `5` is five nanoseconds, and `time.Sleep(5)` requests five nanoseconds, not five seconds. Scheduler timing may make the actual wait longer.

Two more worth knowing on sight: `end.Sub(start)` gives a Duration, and comparing Times uses Before, After and Equal rather than the operators, because a Time carries a monotonic reading as well as a wall clock.
lessons.objective: Write a timeout without wondering what unit it is in.

predict.answer:
1m30s
1.5
36h0m0s
true
predict.question: What does this print? Durations print themselves.

lessons.title: A Duration is a number of nanoseconds with a type

lessons.explanation:
`slices.SortFunc` takes a comparison that returns a negative number, zero or a positive one — not a bool. That trips people coming from languages where the comparator answers "is a before b". `cmp.Compare` does the right thing for any ordered type and is what the comparison should usually be built from.

For a second key, compare the first and fall through only when it is equal. That is the whole pattern, and it is worth writing out once.
lessons.objective: Sort a slice of structs by two keys.
lessons.title: Sorting by whatever you like

lessons.explanation:
A context is how a caller says "stop, I no longer need this". Anything that could block — a network call, a sleep, a channel receive — should take one and should select on `ctx.Done()` alongside whatever it was waiting for. A function that ignores its context is a function nothing can cancel.

`ctx.Err()` says which happened: `context.Canceled` when someone called cancel, `context.DeadlineExceeded` when the timeout ran out. Returning it directly is usually right — the caller already knows what it asked for.
lessons.objective: Make a function that waits stop waiting when told to.
lessons.title: Every blocking call should take a context

lessons.explanation:
Go's own "Writing Web Applications" tutorial and the Tour's "where to go next" both land on `http.Handler`. It is one method:

    ServeHTTP(http.ResponseWriter, *http.Request)

`http.HandlerFunc` turns a function into that type. `http.ServeMux` is a Handler that dispatches to others. The sandbox has no network, so this lesson uses `httptest`: the types are real, the listen is not. A function that accepts `http.Handler` can be tested the same way in any Go module.
lessons.objective: Serve /hello from an in-memory request, with no listen.
lessons.title: http.Handler is one method, like Reader

lessons.explanation:
The Tour's Errors page uses `strconv.Atoi` as the example of a function that returns `(int, error)`. That is the package: no `ParseInt` surprises in everyday code, no `fmt.Sscan` for a single number. `Atoi` is `ParseInt(s, 10, 0)` with a shorter name.

Failure is an error, not a panic and not a zero you are meant to guess at. Discarding that error is how `"x"` becomes port 0.
lessons.objective: Parse a port with Atoi and reject anything outside 1…65535.
lessons.title: strconv is how text becomes a number

lessons.explanation:
`image.Image` describes pixels through three methods: `ColorModel`, `Bounds` and `At`. A decoded PNG produces an image value; the encoded PNG file itself does not implement that interface. A type you write can implement the same pixel contract.

`image/draw` and `image/png` work with image interfaces rather than requiring one concrete bitmap type. This lesson supplies a solid rectangle with chosen bounds and color; encoding that image is a separate step.
lessons.objective: Implement a solid-colour image the standard library will accept.
lessons.title: image.Image is three methods, not a file

lessons.explanation: A byte slice can be a borrowed window rather than an owned result. bytes.Buffer.Bytes exposes unread storage, and Scanner.Bytes exposes a token with a limited lifetime. The type []byte does not express that lifetime. Draw the owner, the view and the next mutation before deciding whether to copy.
lessons.objective: Trace bytes.Buffer and Scanner views, then make retained results independent at a lifetime boundary.
lessons.title: Borrow bytes briefly; copy before their owner changes

lessons.explanation: A JSON object can omit a member, contain null, or contain a concrete zero value. Go fields alone do not always preserve those distinctions. An update that sets enabled to false must not silently become an instruction to leave enabled unchanged. Start with a state table for the operation.
lessons.objective: Choose omitempty, omitzero and request presence models from the endpoint contract.
lessons.title: JSON presence: omitted, zero and null are different states

lessons.explanation: Successful decoding proves only that input was accepted under the decoder policy. It does not authorize the caller or establish a valid business transition. V2 rejects duplicate names and invalid UTF-8 by default; exact field-name matching and unknown-member rejection are separate settings.
lessons.objective: Separate JSON syntax acceptance, unknown-member policy and domain validation.
lessons.title: Strict JSON input: reject ambiguity before side effects

lessons.explanation: Timers have both an API contract and version-dependent implementation behavior. Modern Go timer channels avoid the old buffered stale-value behavior under the documented module/runtime conditions, but this does not let several goroutines reset, receive and decide business state without a protocol. Treat a timer as one owner’s scheduling tool and separately define which events may commit work.
lessons.objective: Explain Stop/Reset behavior, timer ownership and why select is not a priority statement.
lessons.title: Timers and cancellation: versioned semantics still need a single owner

lessons.explanation: A successful Client.Do means an HTTP response was received, not that the application operation succeeded. An error page can still be a valid response, and a server can keep streaming bytes after the headers arrive. Reuse the client and transport, pass an operation context and bound both elapsed time and bytes consumed. Closing the body is necessary even when status handling returns early.
lessons.objective: Own the client lifetime, close bodies and classify HTTP status separately from transport failure.
lessons.title: Outgoing HTTP: reuse the client and bound the response, not just the dial

units.summary: io.Reader and io.Writer, encoding/json, and testing without a framework.
units.title: Standard library patterns
units.translationNote:
Go's survey lists getting more from the standard library as a top friction. The reason is usually not missing knowledge of a package but missing knowledge of two interfaces: once io.Reader and io.Writer click, a surprising share of third-party code stops being necessary.

Some of this unit runs against in-memory transports rather than real sockets, because the sandbox has no network. The compilation and the types are real; only the transport is simulated, and every lesson says so where it applies.

lessons.explanation: Lifetime is the semantic question: how long must a value remain usable? Stack and heap placement are implementation choices used to satisfy that requirement. The compiler performs escape analysis; source syntax alone is not a dependable allocation profiler.
lessons.objective: Explain why returning a local address is safe and why allocation placement must be measured.
lessons.title: Stacks, escape analysis and object lifetimes

lessons.explanation: Garbage collection reclaims memory that the runtime determines is no longer reachable. It does not know that an application has lost interest in a cache entry, nor does it close a forgotten network connection on a useful schedule. Ownership still matters.
lessons.objective: Follow references from roots and distinguish unreachable objects from unwanted live data.
lessons.title: What the garbage collector can and cannot free

lessons.explanation: A service pays for memory in more than one way: live objects occupy space, new allocations create work, and collection uses CPU. Tuning a single GC knob cannot repair an unbounded cache or a queue that retains every request body.
lessons.objective: Distinguish reducing live data from tuning collection frequency and respect a container memory limit.
lessons.title: GC cost, allocation rate and memory budgets

lessons.explanation: A goroutine is a Go execution task scheduled by the runtime. An OS thread is an operating-system execution resource. The runtime multiplexes tasks onto threads; counting goroutines therefore does not tell you how many cores are doing useful work.
lessons.objective: Explain concurrency versus parallel execution without assuming a goroutine is an OS thread.
lessons.title: Goroutines, OS threads and GOMAXPROCS

lessons.explanation: A rising memory graph is a symptom. Before changing code, ask whether traffic grew, objects are retained, workers are stuck, or allocation churn became expensive. Different diagnostic tools answer different questions.
lessons.objective: Choose a heap profile, goroutine profile, CPU profile or trace to test a specific hypothesis.
lessons.title: Find a leak by following evidence

lessons.explanation: Pooling can reduce temporary allocation, but every Get and Put creates an ownership obligation. A former owner must stop using the object after Put. A result that still aliases the object violates that obligation even when the code compiles and a small benchmark looks fast.
lessons.objective: Use sync.Pool with exclusive ownership, independent output and an explicit policy for oversized buffers.
lessons.title: A pool reuses temporary objects; it does not own your results

units.summary: Stacks, GC, goroutines, threads and diagnostic evidence.
units.title: Runtime and memory
units.translationNote: Read worked examples without compiling. Native service behavior can differ from the app's WebAssembly execution environment.

lessons.explanation: A Go web service is more than a route callback. Every request consumes a connection, parsing work, application time and possibly downstream capacity. Give those resources explicit lifetimes. This lesson describes native server code; guest Go programs in the app cannot open network sockets.
lessons.objective: Separate request parsing, domain work, downstream deadlines and response writing.
lessons.title: An HTTP request has a lifecycle and a budget

lessons.explanation: Gin supplies routing, middleware and request/response helpers on top of net/http. It is useful when those conventions reduce repeated adapter code. It does not supply your domain model, persistence policy or downstream capacity, and a small API can also use the standard library.
lessons.objective: Read route groups, path parameters and injected dependencies in a small Gin API.
lessons.title: Gin routes are adapters, not the whole application

lessons.explanation: Decoded JSON is not yet trusted application input. A field can have the right Go type and still violate a business rule. Bound the body, handle decoding failure, then apply domain validation before writing to storage or calling another service.
lessons.objective: Follow JSON binding, size limits, validation and a safe error response.
lessons.title: Validate a request before doing side effects

lessons.explanation: Redis can be overwhelmed by too much work, large payloads, expensive commands or many clients competing for the same resources. Making every slice element a goroutine only moves pressure downstream. Treat the server, the network and the client pool as separate budgets.
lessons.objective: Distinguish client pool limits, request deadlines, rate limits and bounded command batches.
lessons.title: Redis is fast; its capacity is still finite

lessons.explanation: A cache is often added to reduce load, yet its failure path can multiply load. When a popular key expires, many callers may fetch the same value at once. When a timeout triggers retries at several layers, one user action can become many downstream operations.
lessons.objective: Design a cache-miss path that avoids multiplying identical work and ambiguous retries.
lessons.title: Cache misses, retries and overload amplification

units.summary: HTTP, Gin, Redis and the capacity of downstream services.
units.title: Go services
units.translationNote: These reading lessons explain native service designs. They do not add guest network sockets or remote services to the iOS sandbox.

lessons.explanation: Go packages provide namespaces and compile-time dependency boundaries. More packages do not automatically create a cleaner design. Start with behavior that changes together, then separate a boundary when it hides an implementation detail or makes a dependency direction clearer.
lessons.objective: Choose cohesive package boundaries and keep concrete dependencies at the edges.
lessons.title: Packages follow responsibilities, not a diagram

lessons.explanation: Ports and adapters is a way to keep a use case independent of delivery and infrastructure details. It is useful when one behavior has several entry points or storage implementations. The value comes from dependency direction, not from the number of folders named domain.
lessons.objective: Trace an HTTP adapter through an application operation to a storage port and compare test boundaries.
lessons.title: Ports and adapters with a real request

lessons.explanation: Architecture is a choice about boundaries, change and failure. A modular monolith can keep strong internal boundaries with one deployment. Microservices can separate ownership and release schedules, but add remote calls, distributed failures, versioning and operational work.
lessons.objective: Compare a modular monolith, layered design and microservices using concrete operational tradeoffs.
lessons.title: Choose a style; keep the code easy to change

lessons.explanation: Keep a small application understandable without premature service boundaries. A command-line invoice tool can parse input, compute a result and print it in one process. Trace the worked Go example, then compare the benefit with the cost before applying this design to your own project.
lessons.objective: Keep a small application understandable without premature service boundaries.
lessons.title: Simple monolith: start with one executable

lessons.explanation: Separate responsibilities without confusing logical layers with deployed tiers. A layered service routes requests through transport, application logic and persistence. Trace the worked Go example, then compare the benefit with the cost before applying this design to your own project.
lessons.objective: Separate responsibilities without confusing logical layers with deployed tiers.
lessons.title: Layered architecture: transport, application, storage

lessons.explanation: Give business capabilities explicit APIs while retaining local transactions. A modular monolith groups capabilities such as billing and shipping behind package APIs. Trace the worked Go example, then compare the benefit with the cost before applying this design to your own project.
lessons.objective: Give business capabilities explicit APIs while retaining local transactions.
lessons.title: Modular monolith: boundaries inside one deployment

lessons.explanation: Keep domain policy independent of framework and database details. Clean and Onion designs place domain rules near the center and technology at the edge. Trace the worked Go example, then compare the benefit with the cost before applying this design to your own project.
lessons.objective: Keep domain policy independent of framework and database details.
lessons.title: Clean and Onion: dependencies point toward policy

lessons.explanation: Keep feature changes together without duplicating shared invariants. A vertical slice groups request parsing, application behavior and persistence for one capability, such as RenameProject. Trace the worked Go example, then compare the benefit with the cost before applying this design to your own project.
lessons.objective: Keep feature changes together without duplicating shared invariants.
lessons.title: Vertical slices: organize around a use case

lessons.explanation: Model language and invariants before choosing storage or transport. Domain-driven design is a modeling approach, not a demand for microservices. Trace the worked Go example, then compare the benefit with the cost before applying this design to your own project.
lessons.objective: Model language and invariants before choosing storage or transport.
lessons.title: DDD: bounded contexts and aggregates

lessons.explanation: Separate change rules from read shape without assuming two databases. CQRS separates the model that changes state from the model that answers questions. Trace the worked Go example, then compare the benefit with the cost before applying this design to your own project.
lessons.objective: Separate change rules from read shape without assuming two databases.
lessons.title: CQRS: different models for commands and queries

lessons.explanation: Distinguish a source of truth from ordinary logs and notifications. An event-sourced aggregate reconstructs state from accepted domain events. Trace the worked Go example, then compare the benefit with the cost before applying this design to your own project.
lessons.objective: Distinguish a source of truth from ordinary logs and notifications.
lessons.title: Event sourcing: state from a durable history

lessons.explanation: Treat duplicate delivery as normal and define the durable boundary. Event-driven systems decouple a producer from consumers through notifications or durable messages. Trace the worked Go example, then compare the benefit with the cost before applying this design to your own project.
lessons.objective: Treat duplicate delivery as normal and define the durable boundary.
lessons.title: Event-driven services: delivery and idempotency

lessons.explanation: Extract a remote boundary only when its independence is valuable. A microservice owns a business capability, its data and its deployment. Trace the worked Go example, then compare the benefit with the cost before applying this design to your own project.
lessons.objective: Extract a remote boundary only when its independence is valuable.
lessons.title: Microservices: pay for independent ownership

lessons.explanation: Compare service-oriented integration with smaller independently owned services. Service-oriented architecture organizes reusable business capabilities behind contracts, often across existing enterprise systems. Trace the worked Go example, then compare the benefit with the cost before applying this design to your own project.
lessons.objective: Compare service-oriented integration with smaller independently owned services.
lessons.title: SOA and RPC: stable service contracts

lessons.explanation: Compose client-specific views while retaining business ownership. A backend for frontend provides an API suited to a particular client, such as mobile. Trace the worked Go example, then compare the benefit with the cost before applying this design to your own project.
lessons.objective: Compose client-specific views while retaining business ownership.
lessons.title: BFF: an API shaped for one client

lessons.explanation: Separate invocation mechanics from deterministic application behavior. A function platform manages execution capacity while your handler processes an invocation. Trace the worked Go example, then compare the benefit with the cost before applying this design to your own project.
lessons.objective: Separate invocation mechanics from deterministic application behavior.
lessons.title: Serverless handlers: bounded work and retry-safe effects

lessons.explanation: Compose transformations while making backpressure and errors explicit. A pipes-and-filters design passes data through small stages such as decode, validate and transform. Trace the worked Go example, then compare the benefit with the cost before applying this design to your own project.
lessons.objective: Compose transformations while making backpressure and errors explicit.
lessons.title: Pipes and filters: data through independent stages

lessons.explanation: Extend behavior through contracts without assuming dynamic shared libraries. A microkernel or plugin architecture keeps a stable core and accepts extensions through a narrow contract. Trace the worked Go example, then compare the benefit with the cost before applying this design to your own project.
lessons.objective: Extend behavior through contracts without assuming dynamic shared libraries.
lessons.title: Microkernel: a small core with explicit extensions

lessons.explanation: Separate request latency from background completion. A web-queue-worker system accepts a task, durably records it and lets a worker finish later. Trace the worked Go example, then compare the benefit with the cost before applying this design to your own project.
lessons.objective: Separate request latency from background completion.
lessons.title: Web, queue, worker: make slow work durable

units.summary: Compare monoliths, layers, hexagonal and clean designs, DDD, CQRS, events and distributed services.
units.title: Go architectures
units.translationNote: Ratings are editorial fit for a task, not performance measurements. Styles overlap: compare boundaries, consistency and operational cost.

lessons.explanation: Make a caller understand units, results and ownership from the API. Names should reduce guesses at the call site. Trace the worked Go example, then compare the benefit with the cost before applying this design to your own project.
lessons.objective: Make a caller understand units, results and ownership from the API.
lessons.title: Names that expose responsibility

lessons.explanation: Describe a real substitution boundary without wrapping every concrete type. A consumer knows which behavior it needs. Trace the worked Go example, then compare the benefit with the cost before applying this design to your own project.
lessons.objective: Describe a real substitution boundary without wrapping every concrete type.
lessons.title: Small interfaces belong near the consumer

lessons.explanation: Keep failure context useful without logging the same failure at every layer. An error value travels to the layer that can decide what to do: retry, map to a response or stop. Trace the worked Go example, then compare the benefit with the cost before applying this design to your own project.
lessons.objective: Keep failure context useful without logging the same failure at every layer.
lessons.title: Errors: preserve cause and choose one reporting boundary

lessons.explanation: Make it clear whether a caller lends, shares or transfers a buffer. A slice is a view of a backing array, so assignment does not copy its elements. Trace the worked Go example, then compare the benefit with the cost before applying this design to your own project.
lessons.objective: Make it clear whether a caller lends, shares or transfers a buffer.
lessons.title: Ownership: copy mutable data deliberately

lessons.explanation: Turn invalid setup into an explicit startup error. A constructor is a useful boundary for validating configuration that should remain true for an object’s lifetime. Trace the worked Go example, then compare the benefit with the cost before applying this design to your own project.
lessons.objective: Turn invalid setup into an explicit startup error.
lessons.title: Configuration: validate once at construction

lessons.explanation: Test an observable contract with success and failure inputs. A table of cases makes differences explicit without copying the whole test body. Trace the worked Go example, then compare the benefit with the cost before applying this design to your own project.
lessons.objective: Test an observable contract with success and failure inputs.
lessons.title: Behavior tests: tables and boundary cases

lessons.explanation: Separate a behavior-preserving edit from a new requirement. A safe refactor starts with the behavior that must stay stable, then changes one structure at a time. Trace the worked Go example, then compare the benefit with the cost before applying this design to your own project.
lessons.objective: Separate a behavior-preserving edit from a new requirement.
lessons.title: Refactoring: make the safe change small

lessons.explanation: Translate responsibility, substitution and dependency inversion into Go contracts. Single responsibility concerns reasons to change. Trace the worked Go example, then compare the benefit with the cost before applying this design to your own project.
lessons.objective: Translate responsibility, substitution and dependency inversion into Go contracts.
lessons.title: SOLID in Go: principles without class scaffolding

units.summary: Names, interfaces, errors, ownership, tests and safe refactoring.
units.title: Clean code in Go
units.translationNote: Prefer clear concrete code until a real boundary needs abstraction. Follow the worked examples and explain why each change helps.

lessons.explanation: A transport handler can parse a request correctly while the application still commits only half of a business operation. Place the invariant in one use case and make its transaction boundary explicit. The adapter translates HTTP and errors; it does not independently commit each repository call. A Go interface alone cannot make two stores atomic.
lessons.objective: Keep the business invariant and transaction boundary in the application service.
lessons.title: A use case owns its transaction, not its HTTP handler

lessons.explanation: Writing an order and publishing its event are two different side effects. A crash between them can leave a missing event; publishing first can announce a change that never commits. An outbox stores publication intent beside the business write in the same durable transaction. A separate relay retries it, and the consumer expects duplicates rather than claiming end-to-end exactly once.
lessons.objective: Commit a business change and its publication intent together, then deduplicate delivery.
lessons.title: Outbox and inbox: close the database–broker gap

lessons.explanation: A reservation, payment authorization and shipment may belong to different services. They cannot usually share a database transaction. A saga records progress and issues commands whose effects can be retried or compensated. Compensation is another business operation, with its own failures, rather than a database rollback that erases everything that already happened.
lessons.objective: Model a distributed workflow as durable states with explicit compensation and recovery.
lessons.title: Sagas: compensate business steps without pretending to roll back time

lessons.explanation: A rolling deployment is a period with multiple versions, not an instantaneous replacement. The database, producers, consumers and cached clients may all run different code. An additive change is useful only if old readers tolerate it and the new writer does not destroy information they still need. Plan compatibility as a sequence with observable exit conditions.
lessons.objective: Use expand–migrate–contract changes while old and new Go processes coexist.
lessons.title: Evolve APIs, events and schemas across mixed deployments

lessons.explanation: A request can be authenticated and still read another tenant’s object. Authentication proves a principal; authorization decides whether that principal may perform this operation on this resource. Tenant isolation fails when one endpoint is careful but a cache key, bulk export or queued job forgets the same boundary. Treat tenant identity as part of the operation contract.
lessons.objective: Carry a verified tenant identity into storage predicates, cache keys and background jobs.
lessons.title: Tenant isolation belongs in every access path

lessons.explanation: A service can emit millions of log lines while providing no evidence about a failed business operation. Start with a question: is the checkout successful within its time budget, and where is the budget spent? Logs explain individual events, metrics describe distributions and rates, and traces connect sampled work across boundaries. They should share stable operation semantics without sharing every field.
lessons.objective: Connect structured logs, bounded metrics and traces to an explicit service objective.
lessons.title: Observe a Go use case without drowning in cardinality

lessons.explanation: Generated Go stubs remove repetitive transport code, not the need to design a distributed operation. A gRPC method can block, partially stream data, be retried or outlive its caller unless the application defines its lifetime. Treat protobuf fields as a versioned wire contract and the RPC method as a budgeted operation with explicit authorization and failure semantics.
lessons.objective: Define deadlines, stream ownership, status mapping and compatible message evolution.
lessons.title: gRPC and Protobuf: generated methods still need an operational contract

lessons.explanation: A broker can redeliver messages after a consumer crash or partition reassignment. Processing records concurrently makes offset handling more subtle: finishing a later record does not prove that earlier records are durable. Track completion per partition and advance only across the contiguous successful prefix. The business effect needs its own deduplication or transaction protocol.
lessons.objective: Separate message delivery, durable effects and partition-offset ownership.
lessons.title: Kafka-style consumers: commit only a contiguous completed prefix

lessons.explanation: A network partition can prevent replicas from coordinating. Whether a particular operation may proceed depends on the required consistency contract and the available authority, not on whether the service was written in Go or has a cache. Specify which reads may be stale, which writes require a leader or quorum, and what the caller sees when that requirement cannot be met.
lessons.objective: Choose per-operation consistency and failure behavior instead of treating CAP as a product rating.
lessons.title: Consistency under partitions: explain an operation, not a slogan

units.summary: Transactions, outbox/inbox, sagas, compatible changes, tenant isolation and observability.
units.title: Architecture: consistency and evolution
units.translationNote: Work through ownership, durable state and failure recovery. Models distinguish in-memory behavior from the native infrastructure required in production.

lessons.explanation: Dependency injection in Go is usually ordinary constructors and parameters. The important question is not which container library to use but who creates a shared client, who is allowed to close it and how partial startup is cleaned up. Keep wiring near main so a handler cannot silently allocate a new database pool or depend on a hidden global singleton.
lessons.objective: Construct dependencies once and make their ownership and shutdown order explicit.
lessons.title: A composition root makes lifetime and cleanup visible

lessons.explanation: Passing context.Context as the first parameter lets cancellation and deadlines cross a call boundary. It does not force the callee to stop, and it does not prove that a goroutine has exited. Context values are for request-scoped metadata that must cross API boundaries, not an alternative constructor or a hidden transport for required service dependencies.
lessons.objective: Propagate request cancellation while giving detached work an explicit owner and deadline.
lessons.title: Context is a cancellation contract, not a bag of dependencies

lessons.explanation: A repository with packages named controllers, managers and utils can still have no useful boundaries. Ask which behavior changes together and which caller is allowed to depend on it. Go import cycles are prohibited, but a cycle-free graph can still expose every storage struct and force unrelated features to change together. Test the public behavior of a capability, not its current arrangement of private helper calls.
lessons.objective: Use narrow consumer contracts and tests that make accidental coupling visible.
lessons.title: Package APIs should reveal their change boundary

lessons.explanation: An int64 does not tell the next engineer whether it represents milliseconds, Unix seconds, cents or token base units. A float64 cannot represent every decimal amount exactly. At API boundaries, define units, range, rounding and whether a missing field differs from zero. Inside the program, use types and constructors that make those contracts difficult to confuse.
lessons.objective: Separate durations, instants and exact amounts instead of passing ambiguous numbers.
lessons.title: Time and money need units and presence in their types

units.summary: Composition roots, context ownership, package APIs and exact time/money contracts.
units.title: Clean code: production contracts
units.translationNote: Readable Go also needs explicit lifetime, units and failure contracts. These worked examples complement the foundational clean-code unit.

lessons.explanation: Vary product creation without duplicating the algorithm that uses it. The classic Factory Method lets an algorithm ask an overridable creation operation for a product. Trace the worked Go example, then compare the benefit with the cost before applying this design to your own project.
lessons.objective: Vary product creation without duplicating the algorithm that uses it.
lessons.title: Factory Method: supply the creation step

lessons.explanation: Create related products through one selected family. Abstract Factory selects a family of products that should work together. Trace the worked Go example, then compare the benefit with the cost before applying this design to your own project.
lessons.objective: Create related products through one selected family.
lessons.title: Abstract Factory: compatible product families

lessons.explanation: Represent staged construction without making invalid results usable. Builder separates assembly steps from the finished value. Trace the worked Go example, then compare the benefit with the cost before applying this design to your own project.
lessons.objective: Represent staged construction without making invalid results usable.
lessons.title: Builder: assemble then validate

lessons.explanation: Choose shallow or deep copying according to ownership. Prototype creates an object from an existing configured object. Trace the worked Go example, then compare the benefit with the cost before applying this design to your own project.
lessons.objective: Choose shallow or deep copying according to ownership.
lessons.title: Prototype: copy a useful starting value

lessons.explanation: Understand one-instance intent and choose an explicit lifetime. Singleton controls access to one instance. Trace the worked Go example, then compare the benefit with the cost before applying this design to your own project.
lessons.objective: Understand one-instance intent and choose an explicit lifetime.
lessons.title: Singleton: once does not mean global mutable state

units.summary: Factory Method, Abstract Factory, Builder, Prototype and Singleton.
units.title: Patterns: creation
units.translationNote: Classic intent, Go implementation: constructors, function values and composition instead of inheritance.

lessons.explanation: Keep conversion details at the boundary that needs them. An adapter lets an existing implementation satisfy a different caller contract. Trace the worked Go example, then compare the benefit with the cost before applying this design to your own project.
lessons.objective: Keep conversion details at the boundary that needs them.
lessons.title: Adapter: translate one contract into another

lessons.explanation: Compose an abstraction with a separately variable implementation. Bridge separates an abstraction from its implementation so each can vary independently. Trace the worked Go example, then compare the benefit with the cost before applying this design to your own project.
lessons.objective: Compose an abstraction with a separately variable implementation.
lessons.title: Bridge: two independent dimensions of variation

lessons.explanation: Define recursive behavior while guarding the shape of the structure. Composite exposes one operation on both individual values and groups. Trace the worked Go example, then compare the benefit with the cost before applying this design to your own project.
lessons.objective: Define recursive behavior while guarding the shape of the structure.
lessons.title: Composite: treat leaves and groups uniformly

lessons.explanation: Wrap a small operation instead of constructing a type hierarchy. Decorator adds behavior around an object while retaining the interface clients already use. Trace the worked Go example, then compare the benefit with the cost before applying this design to your own project.
lessons.objective: Wrap a small operation instead of constructing a type hierarchy.
lessons.title: Decorator: add behavior while preserving the contract

lessons.explanation: Simplify orchestration without pretending several effects are atomic. A facade offers a convenient operation over several lower-level components. Trace the worked Go example, then compare the benefit with the cost before applying this design to your own project.
lessons.objective: Simplify orchestration without pretending several effects are atomic.
lessons.title: Facade: one useful entry point over a subsystem

lessons.explanation: Separate reusable data from per-use context before optimizing memory. Flyweight shares intrinsic state across many logical objects while callers supply extrinsic context. Trace the worked Go example, then compare the benefit with the cost before applying this design to your own project.
lessons.objective: Separate reusable data from per-use context before optimizing memory.
lessons.title: Flyweight: share immutable intrinsic state

lessons.explanation: Make caching or lazy access preserve the caller’s expectations. Proxy stands in for a real subject and controls access, for example with caching, authorization or lazy construction. Trace the worked Go example, then compare the benefit with the cost before applying this design to your own project.
lessons.objective: Make caching or lazy access preserve the caller’s expectations.
lessons.title: Proxy: control access to an existing operation

units.summary: Adapter, Bridge, Composite, Decorator, Facade, Flyweight and Proxy.
units.title: Patterns: composition
units.translationNote: Follow data ownership and delegated calls. Wrappers should preserve the contracts their callers depend on.

lessons.explanation: Pass interchangeable behavior through a function or small interface. Strategy isolates an algorithm that changes independently of its caller. Trace the worked Go example, then compare the benefit with the cost before applying this design to your own project.
lessons.objective: Pass interchangeable behavior through a function or small interface.
lessons.title: Strategy: choose an algorithm explicitly

lessons.explanation: Make actions queueable or reversible without claiming every effect can be undone. Command packages an operation and its receiver into a value that can be executed later. Trace the worked Go example, then compare the benefit with the cost before applying this design to your own project.
lessons.objective: Make actions queueable or reversible without claiming every effect can be undone.
lessons.title: Command: represent an action as a value

lessons.explanation: Stop or delegate deliberately and make short-circuit order visible. A chain passes a request through handlers that can decide whether to continue. Trace the worked Go example, then compare the benefit with the cost before applying this design to your own project.
lessons.objective: Stop or delegate deliberately and make short-circuit order visible.
lessons.title: Chain of Responsibility: ordered handlers

lessons.explanation: Use iter.Seq or a small Next API and honor early termination. Iterator gives callers sequential access without revealing collection internals. Trace the worked Go example, then compare the benefit with the cost before applying this design to your own project.
lessons.objective: Use iter.Seq or a small Next API and honor early termination.
lessons.title: Iterator: yield values without exposing storage

lessons.explanation: Let participants communicate through a focused coordinator. Mediator moves interaction rules out of a set of objects that otherwise know one another directly. Trace the worked Go example, then compare the benefit with the cost before applying this design to your own project.
lessons.objective: Let participants communicate through a focused coordinator.
lessons.title: Mediator: centralize collaboration deliberately

lessons.explanation: Let the owner define what a valid snapshot contains. Memento stores state so its owner can restore a previous version without exposing editable internals to the caretaker. Trace the worked Go example, then compare the benefit with the cost before applying this design to your own project.
lessons.objective: Let the owner define what a valid snapshot contains.
lessons.title: Memento: retain a restorable snapshot

lessons.explanation: Keep notification lifetime and delivery semantics explicit. Observer lets interested listeners subscribe to changes without the subject knowing their concrete types. Trace the worked Go example, then compare the benefit with the cost before applying this design to your own project.
lessons.objective: Keep notification lifetime and delivery semantics explicit.
lessons.title: Observer: subscribe, notify and unsubscribe

lessons.explanation: Represent legal transitions instead of scattered boolean combinations. State makes behavior depend on an explicit lifecycle state. Trace the worked Go example, then compare the benefit with the cost before applying this design to your own project.
lessons.objective: Represent legal transitions instead of scattered boolean combinations.
lessons.title: State: behavior follows a valid lifecycle

lessons.explanation: Adapt the inheritance-based intent using composition in Go. Template Method defines the order of an algorithm while allowing selected steps to vary. Trace the worked Go example, then compare the benefit with the cost before applying this design to your own project.
lessons.objective: Adapt the inheritance-based intent using composition in Go.
lessons.title: Template Method: fixed workflow, supplied steps

lessons.explanation: Understand the tradeoff between adding node types and adding operations. Visitor separates operations from a stable object structure using dispatch through the node type. Trace the worked Go example, then compare the benefit with the cost before applying this design to your own project.
lessons.objective: Understand the tradeoff between adding node types and adding operations.
lessons.title: Visitor: new operations over a stable set of nodes

lessons.explanation: Model a grammar without treating arbitrary text as executable code. Interpreter represents a grammar with expression nodes and evaluates them against a context. Trace the worked Go example, then compare the benefit with the cost before applying this design to your own project.
lessons.objective: Model a grammar without treating arbitrary text as executable code.
lessons.title: Interpreter: evaluate a deliberately small language

units.summary: Eleven classic patterns, from Strategy and Command to State, Visitor and Interpreter.
units.title: Patterns: behavior
units.translationNote: Introduce machinery only when the variation exists. Each lesson includes a simpler alternative and the cost of the pattern.

lessons.explanation: Control active work instead of starting one goroutine for every input. A worker pool bounds the number of operations in progress. Trace the worked Go example, then compare the benefit with the cost before applying this design to your own project.
lessons.objective: Control active work instead of starting one goroutine for every input.
lessons.title: Worker pool: bound simultaneous work

lessons.explanation: Coordinate multiple producers and one result stream. Fan-out spreads work across producers or workers; fan-in merges their results. Trace the worked Go example, then compare the benefit with the cost before applying this design to your own project.
lessons.objective: Coordinate multiple producers and one result stream.
lessons.title: Fan-out and fan-in: merge without assuming order

lessons.explanation: Make a producer stop when its consumer no longer needs results. Cancellation is a cooperative signal, not a forced goroutine kill. Trace the worked Go example, then compare the benefit with the cost before applying this design to your own project.
lessons.objective: Make a producer stop when its consumer no longer needs results.
lessons.title: Cancellation: propagate an exit path through every handoff

lessons.explanation: Use one goroutine to own mutable state and define request completion. An actor-like owner serializes access to its state through messages. Trace the worked Go example, then compare the benefit with the cost before applying this design to your own project.
lessons.objective: Use one goroutine to own mutable state and define request completion.
lessons.title: Single owner: serialize state through messages

lessons.explanation: Retry transient failures within one deadline without multiplying side effects. A retry repeats an operation that may already have succeeded remotely. Trace the worked Go example, then compare the benefit with the cost before applying this design to your own project.
lessons.objective: Retry transient failures within one deadline without multiplying side effects.
lessons.title: Retry: bounded attempts and idempotent effects

lessons.explanation: Separate retry policy from failure isolation and a controlled recovery probe. A circuit breaker rejects calls after repeated failures, waits for a recovery interval, then permits a probe. Trace the worked Go example, then compare the benefit with the cost before applying this design to your own project.
lessons.objective: Separate retry policy from failure isolation and a controlled recovery probe.
lessons.title: Circuit breaker: stop calls while a dependency recovers

units.summary: Worker pools, fan-in, cancellation, ownership, retries and circuit breakers.
units.title: Patterns: concurrent Go
units.translationNote: Every goroutine needs an owner and an exit path. Production systems also need budgets, observability and failure tests.

lessons.explanation: MongoDB stores BSON documents and the Go driver manages discovery and pools for the deployment. A collection handle is not a new physical connection. Reuse a client across requests, model the fields the application owns, and keep network setup outside request-time package initialization.
lessons.objective: Connect with the Go v2 driver and separate construction, readiness, request work and cleanup.
lessons.title: MongoDB: one client, explicit deadlines and typed documents

lessons.explanation: A query that is fast with ten documents may scan a large collection after real traffic arrives. Shape the filter, sort and returned fields around an actual use case, then inspect the execution plan and the documents examined. Indexes improve selected reads while adding write, memory and maintenance cost.
lessons.objective: Use explain evidence, tenant predicates and stable pagination rather than adding indexes blindly.
lessons.title: MongoDB: design the query and its compound index together

lessons.explanation: Reading a document, changing a field in Go and writing it back leaves a window for another request to change the same value. Memory race detection cannot find that distributed lost update. Express the allowed transition in the database predicate and inspect whether the write actually matched.
lessons.objective: Prevent lost updates with atomic operators and optimistic version checks.
lessons.title: MongoDB: put the invariant in the write predicate

lessons.explanation: A transaction can protect a multi-document invariant, but it adds coordination and can retry work. A callback that charges a card or sends email while updating documents can repeat an external effect. Keep the database transition inside the transaction and move external delivery behind an explicit durable boundary.
lessons.objective: Choose transaction boundaries, concerns and idempotency for ambiguous failures.
lessons.title: MongoDB transactions: retry database work, not external effects

lessons.explanation: A cursor lets an application consume a result in batches; it is not permission to read the entire database without a budget. The query, projection, batch size, total limit and request deadline jointly determine network work and application memory. Check errors after iteration, not only when opening the cursor.
lessons.objective: Avoid loading an unbounded collection into application memory.
lessons.title: MongoDB cursors: bound the result and close the stream

lessons.explanation: When every operation slows down, a larger pool can multiply pressure on the same database. Investigate where the deadline is spent: waiting in the application, selecting a server, checking out a connection, creating a socket or executing a query. Count all application instances and topology servers in the capacity model.
lessons.objective: Separate server selection, pool checkout, query time and application queueing.
lessons.title: MongoDB under load: budget waiting before enlarging the pool

lessons.explanation: Redis is often used as a low-latency data-structure service, but the network, client pool and command cost still exist. Create a shared client, keep a bounded operation context and distinguish redis.Nil from transport failures. A missing optional cache entry and an unavailable required store have different application contracts.
lessons.objective: Configure go-redis deadlines, connection budgets and explicit cache-miss behavior.
lessons.title: Redis: share the client and distinguish a miss from an outage

lessons.explanation: A cache duplicates another source of truth, so freshness and ownership must be explicit. Cache-aside reads can miss together, all query the origin and then repopulate the same key. TTL bounds one kind of staleness; it does not prevent a stampede or make a read-modify-write sequence correct.
lessons.objective: Design expiry, invalidation, negative caching and stampede control deliberately.
lessons.title: Redis cache-aside: TTLs do not solve concurrent fills

lessons.explanation: Pipelining lets a client send multiple commands without waiting for every individual round trip. It can improve throughput for independent work, but it does not make the group indivisible. Large batches also retain commands and replies in memory and can worsen latency for other work.
lessons.objective: Bound command batches, inspect command errors and separate batching from atomicity.
lessons.title: Redis pipelines save round trips; they are not transactions

lessons.explanation: A counter with a timeout and a temporary ownership key look small, but concurrent requests and pauses expose their failure windows. Put dependent steps in one short atomic transition and distinguish an expired lease from a durable guarantee that only one worker can ever act.
lessons.objective: Avoid split increment/expiry races and unsafe lock deletion.
lessons.title: Redis counters and leases need atomic transitions and ownership

lessons.explanation: A consumer group tracks delivery and acknowledgment, not automatic exactly-once application effects. A worker may crash after updating another database but before XACK. Redelivery is useful recovery, so the handler must recognize an operation it has already applied.
lessons.objective: Understand consumer groups, pending entries, redelivery and bounded retention.
lessons.title: Redis Streams: acknowledge after the durable effect

lessons.explanation: Redis command latency can rise because of expensive commands, a hot key, big values, persistence work, network delay or waiting in the client. A low average hides queues and timeout bursts. Correlate request errors with server and client evidence before increasing goroutines or connection limits.
lessons.objective: Inspect server latency and memory while bounding client work and retry amplification.
lessons.title: Redis under load: hot keys, memory pressure and ambiguous retries

units.summary: Clients, queries, atomic writes, caching, streams and behavior under load.
units.title: Around Go: MongoDB and Redis
units.translationNote: Read worked native-service examples here. Run them against an isolated development database on your own machine; these lessons do not add network sockets to the app sandbox.

lessons.explanation: sql.DB is a concurrency-safe pool handle, not a single database connection. Reuse it across the application and close it after its users drain. These lessons describe native Go services using a real driver; the app’s bounded WASI programs cannot open remote database sockets.
lessons.objective: Configure database/sql as a shared pool and measure its actual pressure.
lessons.title: SQL: one pool, explicit capacity and observable waiting

lessons.explanation: A successful QueryContext does not mean every row will decode successfully. Network and server errors can occur during iteration, and Scan can fail on a type or null mismatch. Decide whether partial results are meaningful; do not silently return a successful incomplete list.
lessons.objective: Write a cancellation-aware query loop without losing iteration failures.
lessons.title: SQL rows: close, check errors and bound the result

lessons.explanation: Beginning a transaction does not attach later calls on sql.DB to it. The transaction handle owns a particular transactional connection. A helper that accidentally queries db instead of tx may see another state, escape rollback or wait for a second connection while holding the first.
lessons.objective: Place an atomic business transition inside one explicit transaction owner.
lessons.title: SQL transactions: every participating call uses the transaction

lessons.explanation: A transaction can be atomic without providing the isolation an invariant needs. Two transactions may both read a condition as true and each make a different write that breaks the combined rule. Exact behavior depends on the database and isolation level; this lesson uses PostgreSQL terminology explicitly.
lessons.objective: Explain why atomic statements alone may not preserve a multi-row invariant.
lessons.title: SQL isolation and deadlocks: test the business invariant

lessons.explanation: Retrying the last failed SQL statement can be wrong when an earlier statement read stale state or the transaction is already aborted. A safe retry policy names the driver error, restarts the complete business unit when appropriate, stays within a total deadline and prevents repeated external effects.
lessons.objective: Separate retryable transaction aborts from an ambiguous committed operation.
lessons.title: SQL retries: restart a safe transaction, reconcile an unknown result

units.summary: Shared pools, rows, transactions, isolation, deadlocks and retry-safe commands.
units.title: Around Go: SQL services
units.translationNote: Worked native Go and PostgreSQL examples. Use an isolated database in your own development environment; the app does not open database sockets.

lessons.explanation: A Gin engine is an HTTP adapter with a middleware chain. Group prefixes and registration order decide which handlers participate; the framework does not supply your business transaction. Follow one request before introducing authentication, metrics or error middleware. In particular, Abort stops pending handlers but does not return from the current Go function.
lessons.objective: Explain route groups, middleware order and the difference between Abort and return.
lessons.title: Gin routing and middleware: follow the chain and stop it deliberately

lessons.explanation: Binding converts a request into a Go value. It does not prove authorization or a business invariant, and it does not by itself impose your desired body-size budget. A robust handler limits input first, chooses whether errors are returned or immediately written, validates normalized values and only then calls the use case. Return one deliberate response instead of letting several layers compete to write it.
lessons.objective: Reject oversized or invalid input before performing a business side effect.
lessons.title: Gin input: size limits, binding and business validation are separate

lessons.explanation: Gin reuses contexts after a handler returns. Passing the original *gin.Context into a goroutine can observe another request’s mutable state. Copy is useful for limited read-only context access, but it does not extend the response writer’s lifetime, clone every referenced object or give detached work a durable owner. Prefer extracting immutable job input and handing it to a deliberately managed queue.
lessons.objective: Give background work a bounded owner without keeping a pooled Gin context alive.
lessons.title: Gin contexts and goroutines: extract a job, do not retain the response

lessons.explanation: A reverse proxy may supply the original client address, but a direct client can also send X-Forwarded-For. If a Go service trusts forwarding headers from every peer, address-based controls can be bypassed. Configure exactly which proxy origins are trusted and make the edge replace or sanitize incoming forwarding headers. An IP address remains a network observation, not a user credential.
lessons.objective: Configure proxy trust explicitly and keep client IP separate from authentication.
lessons.title: Trusted proxies: forwarded headers are not proof of identity

lessons.explanation: Framework recovery can keep a panic from crashing a request-serving goroutine, but it cannot undo a committed database write or decide whether a remote operation succeeded. Expected application errors should travel through a deliberate mapping policy. Assign one layer to produce the response, and test both its status and public body rather than checking only that the handler returned.
lessons.objective: Test handler contracts through ServeHTTP without confusing recovery with rollback.
lessons.title: Gin errors and tests: one response owner, explicit failure cases

lessons.explanation: A router handles requests, while net/http.Server owns listener behavior and connection budgets. A short r.Run example is useful for a tutorial, but a deployed service needs an explicit startup and shutdown owner. Readiness, request admission, long-lived streams, background workers and shared clients must fit the same lifecycle rather than each inventing its own stop signal.
lessons.objective: Configure native server timeouts and distinguish HTTP drain from worker completion.
lessons.title: Gin in production: the http.Server owns budgets and shutdown

units.summary: Middleware, bounded input, pooled contexts, proxies, error mapping and native HTTP shutdown.
units.title: Around Go: Gin services
units.translationNote: Worked upstream Gin examples for your native development environment. The app's teaching adapter does not promise every Gin API or network-server capability.

lessons.explanation: Go is used for blockchain nodes and infrastructure, but a backend that reads balances is not the same system as a validator or a signing service. Start with the target network and the operation you must perform. Prefer the protocol’s maintained libraries, inspect their module boundaries and pin a reviewed release. Adding every blockchain SDK increases dependencies without proving correctness.
lessons.objective: Distinguish RPC applications, transaction tooling and consensus/application frameworks.
lessons.title: Go in blockchain: choose packages by the protocol and the job

lessons.explanation: An Ethereum RPC endpoint is an external dependency with latency, availability and trust limits. A successful TCP connection does not prove that the endpoint serves the intended chain or that every call will finish. Use typed clients, time-bounded operations and an expected chain ID configured by the application. Keep node credentials out of logs and never treat RPC data as authenticated business authority by default.
lessons.objective: Use an explicit RPC client, operation deadline and expected chain identity.
lessons.title: Ethereum RPC: verify the chain and bound every operation

lessons.explanation: Token amounts frequently exceed the exact integer range of float64, even when the human-readable value looks small. Converting through a float before math/big permanently loses information. Parse text under an explicit decimal-scale policy, reject unsupported precision and preserve the integer base-unit value. Token metadata is input to validate, not an instruction to allocate unbounded memory.
lessons.objective: Convert validated decimal text to bounded integer base units with an explicit scale.
lessons.title: Token amounts: parse exact base units without float64

lessons.explanation: An ABI describes how to encode a call and decode its result. It does not prove that the target address has the expected code or that a read result will remain true in a future transaction. An eth_call evaluates a call against a selected chain state without committing it. State-changing execution requires a separate signed transaction lifecycle and can fail even after a successful simulation.
lessons.objective: Distinguish ABI packing, read simulation, signed transactions and deployment identity.
lessons.title: Contract ABI: encoding is not permission and eth_call is not a transaction

lessons.explanation: Two Go workers can read the same pending nonce and sign conflicting transactions. A process-local mutex helps only while one process owns the account; it does not coordinate replicas or survive a crash. Give each business intent a stable identity, persist its nonce and signed transaction identity under one ownership protocol, and reconcile unknown send outcomes before allocating new work.
lessons.objective: Coordinate transaction intent and account nonce allocation before retrying a send.
lessons.title: Nonces, fees and unknown outcomes: one durable owner per account

lessons.explanation: A signing key is authority, not an ordinary configuration string. An RPC URL, ABI helper or generic retry function should not automatically receive it. Separate construction and policy validation from key custody, bind transactions to the intended chain, and record what was approved without logging private keys or seed material. Read-only blockchain work does not require a signer at all.
lessons.objective: Validate transaction intent before delegating signing to an explicitly owned key service.
lessons.title: Signing policy: bind the chain and keep key custody separate

lessons.explanation: A WebSocket subscription is a live notification channel, not a durable ledger cursor. A process can disconnect, a provider can drop a slow subscriber and a chain can reorganize recently observed blocks. Store a checkpoint that includes chain identity and block hash, backfill a bounded range after reconnect and make the projection’s rollback or rebuild behavior explicit.
lessons.objective: Persist canonical checkpoints and reconcile removed or missing events before final effects.
lessons.title: Index events through disconnects and reorgs, not just the happy subscription

units.summary: Ethereum, Bitcoin and Cosmos package roles; exact units, RPC, ABI, nonces, key custody and reorg-safe indexing.
units.title: Around Go: blockchain infrastructure
units.translationNote: Developer preparation using local models, reviewed protocol libraries and test environments. This section does not add a wallet, node, signing service or guest networking to GopherForge.

lessons.explanation: A signed token can be genuine and still belong to the wrong audience, issuer or operation. Even a fully valid token does not prove that its subject may read a particular order. Treat authentication as construction of a verified principal and authorization as an explicit resource-scoped decision. Fail closed when either contract is missing rather than accepting whatever identity-shaped value a request provides.
lessons.objective: Validate identity separately from permission to act on a particular resource.
lessons.title: Authentication and authorization: a verified token is only the beginning

lessons.explanation: A fast hash, password hash, MAC, encryption scheme and digital signature answer different questions. A SHA-256 digest does not make a password database resistant to guessing, and encryption without authentication can accept altered ciphertext. Use reviewed libraries and document the purpose, key lifetime, input format and resource budget before selecting a primitive.
lessons.objective: Choose purpose-specific primitives and bound their cost instead of inventing cryptography.
lessons.title: Passwords, MACs and randomness solve different problems

lessons.explanation: A URL supplied by a user can target internal services, metadata endpoints or a different host after redirection. Checking that the string begins with https is insufficient. Prefer a small configured set of upstream services and let user input select a resource within one of them. When arbitrary destinations are a real requirement, enforce address and egress policy at connection time as well as during URL parsing.
lessons.objective: Keep outbound destinations controlled and validate redirects and connection-time policy.
lessons.title: SSRF: let user input choose data, not an arbitrary network destination

lessons.explanation: A TLS connection can encrypt traffic to the wrong peer if verification is disabled. Certificate chain trust and hostname identity both matter; changing a boolean until a development request succeeds can silently remove production authentication. Use a deliberate trust store, keep the expected server identity tied to the configured destination and handle private development certificates through a separate test trust configuration.
lessons.objective: Keep certificate-chain and hostname verification while making trust and rotation explicit.
lessons.title: TLS: verify the peer instead of disabling the error

units.summary: Authentication and authorization, cryptographic purposes, controlled egress and TLS peer identity.
units.title: Around Go: service security
units.translationNote: Apply these patterns in your own native services with an explicit threat model. These lessons do not introduce GopherForge accounts or registration.

lessons.explanation: Claude Code, Codex and Cursor can inspect files, propose patches and run available tools. Useful work still needs a concrete behavior and a way to check it. In this unit you guide an agent in your own repository. Ordinary native projects stay local. The separate Playground adds explicit, opt-in sharing with people and MCP clients; it never uploads an existing project automatically.
lessons.objective: Turn an ambiguous coding request into a small, verifiable Go change.
lessons.title: A Go agent task starts with a contract and a failing example

lessons.explanation: Durable guidance saves repeated explanation of layout, build commands and boundary rules. The supported discovery mechanisms differ between products and can change. Keep the repository facts stable, then consult the official documentation for how the installed tool discovers and scopes them.
lessons.objective: Write useful Go repository instructions without confusing context with permissions.
lessons.title: Repository guidance for Codex, Claude Code and Cursor

lessons.explanation: Generated source can look idiomatic while targeting the wrong driver major version or changing the public result. Compile against the selected module graph, inspect authoritative APIs and test the observable path. A plausible import name or confident explanation is not version evidence.
lessons.objective: Catch invented APIs, unsafe concurrency and changed wire contracts in generated Go.
lessons.title: Verify generated Go against the real module and runtime

lessons.explanation: A source comment, dependency README, test log or fetched webpage can contain instructions written by someone else. Reading that material to solve a Go problem does not authorize its author to expand the task. Keep the user’s goal and trusted repository guidance separate from external diagnostic content.
lessons.objective: Review commands, secrets and external writes when an agent consumes untrusted text.
lessons.title: Agent trust boundaries: repository text is input data

units.summary: Use Codex, Claude Code and Cursor with concrete contracts, repository context and meaningful checks.
units.title: Around Go: coding agents
units.translationNote: Ordinary projects stay local. The separate development Playground adds explicit opt-in MCP sharing; read the guide for local execution and provider boundaries.
